examples.question: Should ARRI develop a differentiated proposition of its own for individual creators, beyond its professional cinema range and its smartphone partnership, or keep its consumer presence to partners? What evidence would justify either choice?

theories.T1: Individual creators will adopt ARRI products if they perceive the brand as a professional standard and are willing to pay a premium for reliability and image quality.
theories.T2: Individual creators will adopt ARRI products if they perceive the brand as a professional standard and are willing to pay a premium for reliability and image quality, but will also be attracted by the smartphone partnership that already provides them with a professional-grade camera and creative control.

arguments.next_action: Run a deposit-backed version of X1: two live offers — a co-branded partner-device upgrade and a reserved direct ARRI creator kit — with refundable deposits as the measure. Fund a direct line only if kit deposits beat the partner offer.
arguments.recommendation: Keep consumer presence to partners (HONOR-style) and do not fund a separate direct-to-individual creator line on this evidence. No source shows creators buying ARRI; ARRI restates high-end cinema as its core focus, and creators use rather than own ALEXA bodies bought by rental houses. A direct premium line would spend against an unproven buyer and risk the exclusivity filmmakers already questioned.
arguments.target_customer: Individual filmmakers and content creators who already rent professional gear for paid work — reached through a partner device rather than sold a cinema body.
arguments.uncertainty: No source measures creator willingness to pay or purchases; HONOR reach is ARRI's claim, not observed adoption. X1's survey figures were analyst constructs and cannot show behaviour.
arguments.value_proposition: ARRI image science, colour and post pipeline inside a partner device at consumer reach, so creators gain creative control without buying a cinema body.
would_change_if: Refundable deposits for a reserved ARRI creator kit match or exceed the co-branded partner offer in the X1 deposit test.
Third-party data or ARRI disclosure shows individual creators buying ALEXA-class bodies, which no source read here shows.
The partner route lapses or fails to convert, removing the channel T2 depends on.

justification.learned: No public source read here shows individual creators buying ARRI. arri-ymc-use-not-own states ALEXA bodies are "commonly purchased by rental houses, studios, and production companies rather than individual creators" — creators use ARRI, not own it, cutting at T1's rental-to-ownership shift. arri-alexa-price puts the launch price far above individual budgets. arri-core-focus restates high-end cinema as core focus; arri-honor-milestone routes consumer reach through HONOR's phone; arri-ymc-backlash shows filmmaker unease at consumer drift. That mix favours T2 (partner reach) over T1 (direct premium ownership), on company assertions and market facts only.
justification.uncertain: Whether creators pay a premium is untested: no source measures willingness to pay or conversion, and X1's offer figures were analyst constructs. arri-honor-milestone is ARRI's claim about reach, not observed adoption; arri-ymc-backlash records reputational risk without sizing it. ARRI is private, so unit sales and creator-segment revenue could not be found. Neither T1 nor T2 has behavioural evidence for its purchase mechanism; a deposit test could still miss repeat use.
justification.why_next: X1 as designed measures stated willingness to pay in a survey — intention, not behaviour, and it cannot show whether a creator who says yes transacts. The cheaper bounded next step is a deposit-backed version of X1: a co-branded partner-device upgrade against a reserved direct ARRI creator kit, with refundable deposits as the measure. That acts on arri-honor-milestone, ARRI's only evidenced consumer channel, and on arri-ymc-use-not-own, where creators rent rather than own, so ownership must be proven with money.

arguments.recommendation: Develop a differentiated direct-to-individual creator proposition (e.g., a new premium camera line) rather than expanding consumer presence beyond existing partnerships.
arguments.target_customer: Individual creators (filmmakers, YouTubers, content creators) who currently rely on rental or lower-cost gear and value professional equipment.
arguments.value_proposition: A premium, professional-grade camera that signals trust and enables ownership, allowing creators to achieve higher-quality results and reduce rental dependency.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed Creator Preference Test (400 creators, 10 weeks, €18,000) to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent for an ARRI direct-to-individual offer versus a HONOR offer. Use the decision rule: if ARRI shows ≥20% higher
arguments.uncertainty: The size of the individual creator market and their willingness to pay a premium for ARRI products are unknown. The smartphone partnership already provides a functional advantage, so it may not be necessary for a new direct proposition.
would_change_if: If the test shows ARRI willingness to pay significantly below HONOR or purchase intent below 5 points, we would reconsider the direct proposition and explore alternative models.
If new evidence shows strong demand for ARRI among individual creators or a clear path to capture value beyond the smartphone partnership, we would revise the recommendation.

examples.review_note: A final recommendation should stay bounded: refuse to fund a direct product line on company assertions or survey-based stated preference, and instead convert the survey into a deposit-backed, behaviour-revealing test with two genuinely different live offers and a clear go/no-go threshold. It also shows correct evidence handling: each cited source is weighed for what it actually shows (creators use/rent rather than own; partner reach is a claim, not observed adoption), and the answer states concrete conditions that would change the call.

examples.question: Should Koppert develop a differentiated proposition for home gardeners, building on its biological crop protection for professional growers, or stay with professional growers? What evidence would justify either choice?

theories.T1: Home gardeners will adopt Koppert's biological controls if they perceive them as convenient, easy to use, and safe for children and pets, leading to higher purchase frequency and willingness to pay a premium.
theories.T2: Home gardeners will adopt Koppert's biological controls if they perceive them as a status symbol or a way to differentiate their garden, leading to higher purchase frequency and willingness to pay a premium.

arguments.next_action: Run a bounded real-sale pilot: one beneficial SKU in retail packs through a small number of garden centres over 12 weeks within the €20,000 envelope, recording unit sales, price paid and repeat purchase instead of stated intent.
arguments.recommendation: Keep the home-gardener option open but do not build a retail proposition yet. Koppert already sells to home gardeners (koppert-lo-canada, koppert-martha-visit), but no evidence read shows demand, price paid or repeat purchase. Test commercially first with one beneficial SKU sold through existing retail within the €20,000 / 12-week analyst envelope, and commit only if buyers repeat.
arguments.target_customer: Existing home-gardener buyers of beneficial insects — the "home gardening enthusiast" Koppert Canada already serves and hobby gardeners who buy biologicals for their own plots, not institutional clients.
arguments.uncertainty: No source read measures home-gardener demand, willingness to pay or repeat purchase, and channel economics and brand transfer are unverified; demand is unknown.
arguments.value_proposition: Beneficial insects presented as simple, ready-to-apply and safe for children and pets, carrying Koppert's professional biocontrol credibility into retail packs rather than sold as a status object.
would_change_if: A real-sale pilot shows buyers returning for a second purchase and paying more than for generic chemical options, which would strengthen T1.
Retail sales stall and buyers describe a one-off or display purchase, which would weaken T1 and favour staying with professional growers.
Evidence that home gardeners find beneficials fiddly or unreliable (e.g. lady beetles dispersing) would undercut the convenience mechanism behind T1.

justification.learned: Koppert already reaches individual buyers, so the question is differentiation, not entry: its Canadian subsidiary supplies \"both the professional grower and the home gardening enthusiast\" (koppert-lo-canada), its staff built a pest plan for Martha Stewart's private Bedford farm (koppert-martha-visit), and lady beetles are \"shipped to farmers and home gardeners alike\" (koppert-wsu-shipped). T1 is favoured only weakly: a standing dual grower/hobbyist channel fits a convenience-and-safety mechanism better than a prestige one, while T2's only support is one prestige client. Nothing read measures demand, price or repeat purchase, so this is mechanism plausibility, not observed demand.
justification.uncertain: Home-gardener demand, willingness to pay and repeat purchase are unknown — no source read measures them; koppert-martha-visit is one prestige customer and koppert-wsu-shipped only describes shipping. Whether Koppert's professional credibility transfers to retail buyers, and whether garden-centre or direct channels would carry biologicals profitably, is unestablished. No financial data is in the dossier, so margins and channel costs could not be found.
justification.why_next: X1 as designed varies only packaging message and records stated purchase intent, so it cannot show whether anyone buys or comes back — it should not be run as written. The bounded alternative is a real-sale pilot of one beneficial SKU through a few retail outlets inside the brief's €20,000 / 12-week envelope, measuring units sold, price paid and repeat purchase; that separates T1 (repeat buying driven by ease and safety) from T2 (one-off display purchase) and decides whether the proposition is worth building. koppert-lo-canada and koppert-wsu-shipped are the only weighed support for T1.

arguments.recommendation: Develop a differentiated home-gardener proposition that emphasizes convenience, safety, and ease of use, leveraging Koppert’s existing professional reputation to build trust. Use retail packaging and direct-to-consumer channels to reach home gardeners, while monitoring actual purchase behavior throu…
arguments.target_customer: Home gardeners who grow vegetables, fruits, or flowers and are willing to adopt biological controls as an alternative to chemical pesticides.
arguments.value_proposition: A convenient, safe, and easy-to-use retail package of biological controls (e.g., lady beetles) that delivers effective pest control without chemical residues, positioned as a trusted professional‑grade solution for the home gardener.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed Home Gardener Proposition Test (500 respondents, 10 weeks, €15,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for convenience‑focused versus status‑focused packages.
arguments.uncertainty: Actual purchase behavior and willingness to pay for a convenience‑focused proposition; the extent to which home gardeners value status signaling; and the feasibility of reaching home gardeners through retail channels.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for the convenience package is at least 20 percentage points higher than for the status package, or if willingness to pay for convenience exceeds status by a significant margin, we would shift toward a T1‑

If the test shows no meaningful difference or status package outperforms convenience, we would reconsider the strategy and possibly explore a status‑focused proposition or stay with professional growers.
If new evidence shows strong home‑gardener demand for biological controls driven by status signaling, we would revise the recommendation to prioritize a status‑focused proposition.

examples.question: It is 1983. Should Mag Instrument develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its machined anodized-aluminium flashlights? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Civilians will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition because they perceive the Maglite as a status symbol and a symbol of professional reliability, leading them to purchase multiple units for personal use.
theories.T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition because they need reliable, professional‑grade flashlights for outdoor recreation and home safety, and they will purchase multiple units to ensure availability.

arguments.next_action: Bounded step: gather pre-1983 retail trade records — which chains stock the light, sell-through, reorders, returns, cited use cases — and review them before committing to any consumer variant.
arguments.recommendation: Do not commit to a differentiated consumer proposition on this evidence. Keep the public-safety business as the core and treat civilian retail as an unproven option. What would justify the investment is observed civilian behaviour at premium prices — sell-through and reorders where the light already sells, plus confirmed use cases. The police-issue association is a positioning asset, not proof of demand.
arguments.target_customer: Undetermined. No weighed source identifies which civilians buy Maglites or for what use case; the status-seeking buyer (T1) and the outdoor/home-safety buyer (T2) remain hypotheses.
arguments.uncertainty: Civilian demand, price paid and use case are unknown; no dossier source reports them, and X1 could not separate the two causes.
arguments.value_proposition: Professional-grade reliability borrowed from police issue, offered to civilians only once evidence shows they pay a premium; no use-case claim is yet supported.
would_change_if: Sell-through and reorder records show civilians buying at premium prices and repeating, supporting T1's status mechanism over T2's functional one.
Records show the light reaches buyers only through public-safety channels, so no civilian proposition is warranted now.
A pre-1983 trade or consumer source names a specific use case (outdoor or home safety) actually driving purchases.

justification.learned: No assessed source shows civilian demand, so the case rests on positioning, not observed buying. T1's only weighed support is mag-amw-standard ("The Maglite is a powerful and durable flashlight and for many years was the standard issued gear used by police officers in the USA") — that lends a professional reputation to borrow, but does not show civilians pay a premium for status. mag-fu-civilians ("The flashlight also was designed to be attractive to civilians") was neutral for T2: design intent is not purchase or use case. The T1 challenge found nothing against it, which is not support. SYN-D bore on neither theory and was kept. T1 favoured weakly.
justification.uncertain: Whether any civilian segment pays a premium is unknown: no weighed source reports civilian purchases, prices paid or a specific use case, so T1 and T2 both stay uncertain and X1 could not separate them because it varies only message framing. Claims about retail placement and mass-market sales sit in mag-fu-stores and mag-nbc-mass, read but never weighed and written long after 1983, so they cannot carry a 1983 decision. Financial data is absent from the dossier entirely.
justification.why_next: The missing link behind T1 (mag-amw-standard) and T2 (mag-fu-civilians) is behavioural: do civilians buy at premium prices and repeat? X1 answers that with a message-framing survey, which cannot separate a status buyer from a functional one, so it should not be run. The bounded step is documentary: pull pre-1983 retail/trade records on the product — chains stocking it, sell-through, reorders, returns — and review them before any consumer variant is designed. If that shows premium civilian repeat buying, revisit the proposition; if only public-safety distribution, stay with B2B.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for civilians that emphasizes the Maglite’s professional‑grade reputation and status appeal, targeting outdoor enthusiasts and homeowners. Use premium pricing and specialty retail channels to capture higher margins.
arguments.target_customer: Individual consumers seeking reliable, high‑performance flashlights for outdoor activities, home safety, and personal projects.
arguments.value_proposition: A premium‑grade Maglite marketed as a status symbol of professional reliability, offering durability, professional‑grade performance, and a unique brand identity, sold through specialty retailers and direct‑to‑consumer channels.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed Maglite Consumer Demand Test (500 U.S. adults, 10‑week survey) to validate willingness to pay thresholds and purchase intent for a premium‑grade Maglite.
arguments.uncertainty: The size of the civilian market willing to pay a premium for a professional‑grade flashlight is unknown. Evidence of actual purchase behavior is limited to B2B use; there is no public data on civilian demand or price sensitivity in 1983.
would_change_if: If the test shows willingness to pay below 15% premium or purchase intent below 30% for a differentiated Maglite, the investment would be reconsidered in favor of a generic consumer proposition or no expansion.

examples.question: It is mid-2014. Should ResMed develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its non-contact sleep-sensing technology and sleep-medicine expertise? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Individuals with sleep apnoea will adopt a home sleep test device if they perceive it as convenient and accurate, and if they are willing to pay a premium for non-contact technology that avoids the need for clinic visits.
theories.T2: Insurance companies will cover home sleep tests if they are validated against polysomnography and demonstrate clinical efficacy, leading consumers to adopt home testing because they avoid clinic visits and reduce out-of-pocket costs.

arguments.recommendation: Do not commit to consumer development yet. As of mid-2014 no source read shows consumer demand, willingness to pay or payer coverage for home testing; the evidence weighed for T1 (resmed-10k-clinics) describes a clinician and dealer channel, and products are typically resold to patients by a dealer. Fund a bounded behavioural test within the 20000-euro, 12-week analyst budget before any development spend.
arguments.target_customer: Adults with suspected or diagnosed sleep apnoea who today reach care through sleep clinics, non-sleep specialist physician practices, or a home healthcare dealer that resells the device to them (resmed-10k-clinics, resmed-10k-dealer).
arguments.value_proposition: Non-contact, touch-free measurement of sleep and breathing at home, backed by clinical validation against polysomnography, positioned on convenience rather than as a diagnostic replacement until accuracy is proven.
arguments.next_action: Run X1 as a real-money deposit offer in one channel at a premium and a low price, not a stated-intent survey; proceed only if premium-price conversion reaches X1's threshold, otherwise stop.
arguments.uncertainty: Whether individuals with sleep apnoea pay a premium out of pocket, and whether payers would cover home testing, are both unmeasured; sensor agreement is moderate (kappa 0.38) and no financial data is available.
would_change_if: Premium-price deposits in X1 reach the willingness-to-pay and intent thresholds set for T1, showing out-of-pocket buyers exist at scale.
A payer or dealer commits to reimbursement or volume for the sensor, which would support T2 over T1.
Independent validation shows the sensor agreeing with polysomnography strongly enough in high-AHI patients to be used diagnostically.

justification.learned: T1 survives only weakly. The one source weighed for it, resmed-10k-clinics, shows ResMed markets to home healthcare dealers, sleep clinics and physician practices — a clinician/dealer channel, not individual buyers; resmed-10k-dealer (read) confirms a dealer buys and resells to the patient. resmed-pr-biancamed, the source weighed for T2, is only a company assertion that the sensor is "accurate, touch-free". Neither shows consumer demand, willingness to pay or insurer coverage, so demand is unknown. resmed-pm-dechazal2011 (read) reports 78% accuracy and kappa 0.38, worse at AHI>15, so the accuracy premise is modest. X1 is designed but unrun.
justification.uncertain: Everything about buyers is unknown: no source read measures willingness to pay, purchase or payer reimbursement as of mid-2014, and no financial data is in the dossier. T1 rests on a channel description (resmed-10k-clinics); T2 has no evidence of insurer behaviour at all — resmed-pr-biancamed speaks to sensor capability only, not coverage. Whether moderate agreement with polysomnography (kappa 0.38, resmed-pm-dechazal2011) is diagnostic enough is untested.
justification.why_next: The demand side is completely unmeasured, so the cheapest next step is a bounded behavioural test, not a build. T1 says individuals pay a premium for non-contact convenience; T2 says adoption follows third-party coverage, keeping out-of-pocket price sensitivity high. X1 already sets different predictions for each (premium price with high intent under T1, low price with low intent under T2), but as a stated-intent survey it cannot show either mechanism, so run it as a real-money deposit ask. resmed-10k-clinics and resmed-10k-dealer show the current route runs through dealers and clinics, which is why a real-money offer in one channel is the discriminating move.

examples.question: Should Cotral Lab develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing hearing-protection offering? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Professional musicians will adopt custom-moulded hearing protection if it is marketed as a performanceenhancing tool that preserves sound quality while blocking noise, because they value accurate sound and are willing to pay a premium for a product that does not compromise their craft.
theories.T2: Sleep aid users will adopt custom-moulded hearing protection if it is marketed as a medical-grade solution that reduces sleep disruption caused by background noise, because they seek a product that addresses a specific health concern and are willing to pay for a solution that improves sleep quality.

arguments.next_action: Add a real-money arm to X1: refundable deposits on the same musician and sleep-aid offers through each group's own channel, inside X1's estimated €15,000 and 10 weeks.
arguments.recommendation: Hold rather than build a consumer proposition now. Cotral's evidenced strengths are employer channels and in-house filter and connectivity engineering (ctl-deal, ctl-onsite, ctl-filter, ctl-it1); no source shows individuals buying custom moulds, and the one independent study found comfort and looks, not sound quality, drove musician appreciation. Keep the B2B base and settle consumer demand with a bounded test first.
arguments.target_customer: Professional and semi-professional musicians buying protection for rehearsal and live performance — the group where T1's mechanism has any independent support; consumer willingness to pay is unproven for both groups.
arguments.uncertainty: Consumer demand is unknown: no source shows Cotral selling to individual buyers, and no price, volume or conversion figure was found.
arguments.value_proposition: Custom-moulded protection whose in-house filters lessen noise on specific frequencies while keeping the performance audible (ctl-filter), framed as craft-preserving rather than generic safety gear.
would_change_if: A deposit pilot where musicians convert to paid pre-orders far more than sleepers would reverse the hold and justify a musician line (X1).
Evidence that Cotral already sells direct to individual buyers at scale would remove the channel gap and raise T1.
Independent data showing sound quality outranks comfort and looks for musician buyers would weaken the bockstael-2015-looks finding behind the hold.
Credible evidence that noise-disrupted sleepers pay for custom moulds would raise T2.

justification.learned: Cotral is the world No.1 in custom-moulded protection and a prescription safety-eyewear player, now owned by PPE distributor Groupe RG (ctl-deal). Its evidenced differentiation is engineering plus an employer route: in-house frequency filters (ctl-filter), Bluetooth-connected IT1 for employees (ctl-it1), impressions taken on-site for employees (ctl-onsite). None of that shows consumer demand. The only independent observation in the dossier, bockstael-2015-looks, found appreciation "mainly depended on comfort and looks, while differences in sound quality were less noticeable" — that weakens T1's core mechanism. T1 is favoured only because T2 has no evidence at all.
justification.uncertain: Whether individual consumers are a viable market at all: no source shows Cotral selling to individuals, and I found no price, volume, revenue or conversion figure; the brief warns financials may not be public. T2's health framing is untested. I could not check whether Cotral's in-house filters stand out against consumer earplugs, since the one remaining unread result was not readable within the search budget.
justification.why_next: X1 is the only design that pits T1 against T2 on one measure, but it records stated willingness to pay, and the evidence base (ctl-deal, ctl-filter, ctl-it1) shows capability rather than purchase, so stated numbers cannot carry the decision. Keep X1's comparison but add a real-money arm. ctl-onsite and ctl-deal also show revenue runs through employers, so any consumer offer needs a new channel — that is the real cost behind the hold.

examples.question: It is mid-2025. Should Netafim develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its drip-irrigation technology? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Home gardeners will adopt Netafim's drip irrigation kits because they perceive the technology as a medical necessity for plant health, leading them to purchase multiple kits for different plants.
theories.T2: Home gardeners will adopt Netafim's drip irrigation kits because they value convenience and time savings, leading them to purchase kits for multiple plants or spaces.

arguments.recommendation: Do not commit to a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The only differentiated asset evidenced is water efficiency (over 90 percent versus 50 to 70 percent for sprinklers), and Netafim already sells a home garden kit in India; no source shows that gardeners buy it, pay a premium, or that plant-health framing drives purchase. Fund evidence of real purchases first.
arguments.target_customer: Home gardeners with small plots, terraces, balconies and kitchen gardens who install irrigation themselves; the group Netafim's India garden kit and non-expert guidance already address.
arguments.value_proposition: Water delivered to plants at over 90 percent efficiency, against 50 to 70 percent for sprinklers, in a kit a non-expert can install. Whether a home gardener pays a premium for that is untested.
arguments.next_action: Supersede X1 with a bounded live purchase test: offer the existing garden kit at one fixed retail price in a single market for 12 weeks within the 20000 euro budget, and count actual purchases and repeat or multi-unit orders.
arguments.uncertainty: No source shows consumer sales, retail distribution, price or repeat purchase for Netafim kits; group revenue ($1.063bn in 2019) is not split by segment, so consumer demand and willingness to pay are unknown.
would_change_if: A live fixed-price offer produces real purchases above competing kits with repeat or multi-unit buying, making a proposition worth building on T1 or T2.
Sell-through evidence shows Netafim's existing India garden kits already sell in volume, which would favour expansion over staying B2B.
Purchases appear only at parity pricing with no repeat buying, which would favour no consumer expansion.

justification.learned: Evidence is thin. netafim-csu-efficiency (independent study) shows drip exceeds 90 percent efficiency versus 50 to 70 percent for sprinklers: engineering capability, not a buying motive. netafim-in-homekit and netafim-in-nonexpert show Netafim India already sells Garden drip kits for home gardens, terraces, balconies and kitchen gardens, pitched at non-experts: an existing consumer offer, not proof it sells. netafim-wiki-revenue gives only group revenue. T1 and T2 are not separated by this dossier: T1's record rests on the efficiency study, which cannot show a medical-necessity motive, and T2's on a product page; X1 varies only message.
justification.uncertain: Unknown: any consumer revenue, unit sales, retail distribution, price or repeat purchase; whether plant health or time saving drives a gardener's purchase. T1 and T2 both lack motive evidence, and X1 would measure stated intent under different framings, not purchases. Group revenue ($1.063bn in 2019) is not split by segment, and no source is dated to confirm what was true in mid-2025.
justification.why_next: Neither T1 nor T2 has evidence of motive (netafim-csu-efficiency and netafim-in-homekit bear at most on capability and on an existing consumer kit), so T1 drops from likely to uncertain and the state's 'supports' call for T1 was generous. X1 varies only framing and measures stated intent, so running it would not separate the two mechanisms. The call acts on X1 by superseding it: buy consequential evidence, actual purchases and repeat orders at a fixed price, before any proposition investment.

examples.question: It is March 2016. Should Embrace Innovations develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its infant-warming technology? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Parents of low‑birth‑weight infants will adopt a home‑use infant warmer if they perceive it as a medical necessity that reduces the risk of SIDS and is affordable, because they are willing to pay a premium for a product that addresses a serious health concern.
theories.T2: Parents of low‑birth‑weight infants will adopt a home‑use infant warmer if they perceive it as a convenient, affordable way to monitor their baby’s temperature and health at home, because they value time‑saving and ease of use, and are willing to pay a price that reflects the convenience.

arguments.recommendation: Do not fund a differentiated consumer proposition yet: the dossier shows a working direct channel but no evidence of demand for a home warmer. Keep the clinical/B2B warmer and fund one bounded behavioural test — refundable deposits through the existing direct-to-consumer channel — before any product investment. Any consumer offer should lead on infant warmth and health risk, the only consumer benefit a source names.

arguments.next_action: Run a refundable-deposit pre-order through the existing direct channel, health vs convenience framing at two price points, measuring deposits and conversion to paid order over 12 weeks; stop below the pre-set deposit threshold.
arguments.uncertainty: Demand, price and volume for a consumer warmer are unshown in every source read; the SIDS benefit is a company claim, not a clinical finding; convenience has no evidence; buyer and geography are open; no financial data exists.

arguments.value_proposition: A home infant warmer that provides safe, controlled warming and monitoring, backed by medical claims of reduced SIDS risk, sold at a premium price that reflects the health benefit and convenience of home use.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed Parent Preference Survey (300 parents, 8 weeks, €15,000) to test whether medical necessity drives purchase intent. Use the results to decide whether to proceed with a full consumer launch or refine the proposition.

would_change_if: If the survey shows convenience ranking higher than medical necessity with a ≥2-point difference, we would shift focus to a convenience‑focused proposition and lower the price point.

If a competitor launches a similar product with a clear health‑focused message, we would reassess the market fit.

examples.question: Should ARRI develop a differentiated proposition of its own for individual creators, beyond its professional cinema range and its smartphone partnership, or keep its consumer presence to partners? What evidence would justify either choice?

theories.T1: Individual creators will adopt ARRI products if they perceive the brand as a professional standard and are willing to pay a premium for reliability and image quality.
theories.T2: Individual creators will adopt ARRI products if they perceive the brand as a professional standard and are willing to pay a premium for reliability and image quality, but will also be attracted by the smartphone partnership that already provides them with a professional-grade camera and creative control.

arguments.quote: For most filmmakers, ARRI has always been a brand they use rather than a brand they own. ALEXA cameras sit at the top of the professional cinema market, commonly purchased by rental houses, studios, and production companies rather than individual creators.
arguments.does_not_show: It cannot show willingness to pay or whether a differentiated, cheaper direct offer would change rental habits; it describes the current channel, not response to a new product.

justification.learned: ARRI's own statements confine it to "the high-end cinema and live entertainment markets" (arri-core-focus), its newest body is a $55,000 Alexa 35 Xtreme (arri-alexa-price), it is cutting jobs as production volumes fall (arri-cined-challenges), and its stated route to individual creators is the HONOR smartphone imaging partnership (arri-honor-milestone). Every source so far describes capability, positioning or company intent; none measures demand. T1's distinctive premise is behavioural: that individual creators would shift from renting to owning. arri-ymc-use-not-own is the only source I read that describes who actually buys ARRI cameras, which is exactly the claim T1 turns on.
justification.uncertain: Whether any demand exists. No source I read reports individual creators' purchase intent, willingness to pay, or the size of that segment; ARRI's financials are private. Whether a cheaper or differentiated line would change rental habits is untested. The Y.M.Cinema characterisation is a magazine's summary of channel structure, not a measured survey, so it fixes the status quo (rental/studio purchasing) but says nothing about response to a new offer.
justification.why_next: Weigh arri-ymc-use-not-own against T1, because if the rental-to-ownership premise fails, T1 must be revised before any test is designed around it. One challenge search is kept in reserve to look specifically for evidence of individual creators buying cinema cameras outright.

examples.question: It is mid-2014. Should ResMed develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its non-contact sleep-sensing technology and sleep-medicine expertise? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Individuals with sleep apnoea will adopt a home sleep test device if they perceive it as convenient and accurate, and if they are willing to pay a premium for non-contact technology that avoids the need for clinic visits.
theories.T2: Insurance companies will cover home sleep tests if they are validated against polysomnography and demonstrate clinical efficacy, leading consumers to adopt home testing because they avoid clinic visits and reduce out-of-pocket costs.

arguments.quote: The S+ will be available for the suggested retail price of $149.99 at Bed Bath & Beyond® stores beginning in mid-October and online at mysplus.com .
arguments.does_not_show: No purchase, adoption, willingness to pay or reason to buy is shown, and S+ is a consumer sleep tracker rather than an apnoea test; the release also postdates mid-2014, so it was not knowable at the decision point.

justification.learned: The dossier holds only ResMed's own words. resmed-10k-clinics shows the FY2014 model: products marketed "primarily to home healthcare dealers and to sleep clinics", a B2B route with no direct-to-individual channel. resmed-pr-biancamed shows capability only: a non-contact sensor "validated against polysomnography in clinical studies". resmed-pr-splus is the nearest consumer item: retail at $149.99 via Bed Bath & Beyond. T1 (consumers pay a premium for convenience) and T2 (payer coverage drives adoption) rest on company claims only; no customer observation, independent study or market sizing — demand is unknown.
justification.uncertain: No source I read shows anyone actually bought, used or asked for a consumer sleep device from ResMed, and none shows willingness to pay. resmed-pr-splus also postdates the mid-2014 decision point (dated 2014-10-07), so it cannot be treated as knowledge available to the decision; and S+ is positioned as a consumer sleep tracker, not a diagnostic test for apnoea, so even as a company claim it addresses a different use case than T1's. Whether payers reimburse home testing (T2) is likewise unread.
justification.why_next: I weigh resmed-pr-splus on T1, the only read source touching individual buyers, price and retail channel. As company_assertion it is neutral on T1: a retail price and partner show ResMed could reach consumers at a premium point, informing feasibility and positioning, but not why anyone buys, whether apnoea patients would substitute it for a clinic study, or whether $149.99 is acceptable. Since T1 rests on company claims, the next step (2 searches left) is a non-company source on consumer behaviour or payer coverage; resmed-10k-dealer may show how the dealer channel could carry a consumer device.

examples.question: It is early 2015. Should Osram Licht AG develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its LED and lighting technology? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Consumers will adopt smart LED lighting if they perceive it as a convenience that saves time and effort, because they value ease of use and automation.
theories.T2: Consumers will adopt smart LED lighting if they perceive it as a cost‑saving solution that reduces electricity bills, because they value financial return and energy efficiency.

arguments.quote: The coloured bulb retails for £39.99, which is £10 less than the Philips Hue alternative, with the Lightify Gateway priced at £39.99 as well.
arguments.does_not_show: It gives a price and a rival comparison, not why anyone bought; it cannot show that convenience or automation drove purchase, only that Osram priced below Hue in a market where Hue already existed.

justification.learned: Reads so far: the company already reaches individual buyers — osram-li14-consumer (company claim) puts "products for consumers" inside its Luminaires & Solutions segment, and osram-wiki-sylvania says Osram Sylvania sells "for homes, business, and vehicles". A consumer route therefore exists, but it is a general lighting-bulb business: osram-ldv-april and osram-ee-40 show that business was over a third of the workforce and ~40% of turnover (~€2bn in FY2015), and it was being divested (announced April 2015). osram-tr-hue gives the only product-level market fact: Osram's Lightify coloured bulb at £39.99, £10 below Philips Hue, gateway £39.99 — a premium positioning against an incumbent.
justification.uncertain: No source shows why anyone bought, or would buy, a smart bulb: osram-li14-consumer is a segment description, not demand. Whether convenience/automation (T1) or bill savings (T2) drives purchase is untested, and price sensitivity at £39.99 per bulb is unknown. osram-l12-mckinsey forecasts market growth, not consumer motivation.
justification.why_next: Weigh osram-tr-hue against T1 with assess_evidence: it is third-party trade press (market_fact), not the company speaking, and it is the only source giving Osram's actual consumer price point versus a rival — exactly what T1's premium-pricing mechanism depends on. It shows the proposition existed and was priced below Hue, but not that convenience persuaded anyone to buy.

examples.question: It is early 2003. Should Quantum Devices, Inc. develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its high-intensity LED light sources for medical research and military first aid? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Consumers will adopt home photodynamic therapy LED devices if they view them as a medical necessity for skin conditions like acne or psoriasis, and the device is marketed as a safe, FDA-cleared solution.
theories.T2: Consumers will adopt home photodynamic therapy LED devices if they view them as a convenient, at‑home alternative to clinical treatments, and the device is marketed as a quick‑fix for skin conditions.

arguments.does_not_show: It shows no consumer purchase of any LED device and no effect of enforcement on cleared devices; it therefore cannot establish whether medical-necessity framing sells, only that unsubstantiated health claims to consumers carried legal risk.
arguments.quote: "Operation Cure.All," targets companies touting bogus cancer cures and making unsubstantiated health claims, such as "magnetic therapy devices" can alleviate arthritis and high blood pressure.

justification.learned: T1 claims individuals buy a home LED device because they treat it as a medical necessity backed by FDA clearance. Sources read so far: qdi-fda-k032229 shows a clearance exists (K032229, "QUANTUM WARP 10 LIGHT DELIVERY SYSTEM") but under the classification "Lamp, Infrared, Therapeutic Heating" — capability and regulatory route, not demand. qdi-pm-mucositis2002 reports "There were no significant differences between sides in OMI or pain", so the clinical basis is thin. qdi-sp22-homesplit and qdi-sp22-exit are post-2003. No source yet records a consumer buying anything. qdi-ftc-cureall adds that the consumer health-claim channel T1 depends on was enforced against in 1999.
justification.uncertain: Whether any consumer in 2003 would pay for such a device: zero demand evidence exists in the dossier for T1 (or T2). No price, margin, unit-volume or channel data (the brief confirms financials are absent). Unclear how far FTC enforcement reached legitimately cleared devices, so I cannot size the constraint on T1's "medical necessity" framing. Whether qdi-fda-k032229's heating-lamp classification would even permit skin-treatment marketing is unresolved.
justification.why_next: Weighing qdi-ftc-cureall against T1 as a regulation source: it bears on T1's assumption that safety/efficacy claims can simply be communicated to buyers, but it concerns bogus cancer cures, not LED skin devices, and records no buyer behaviour, so it constrains without confirming or refuting the purchase mechanism. Next, T1 needs non-company behavioural evidence — ideally a customer_observation source on home light devices — and then a challenge search against qdi-fda-k032229's implication of easy consumer clearance.

examples.question: It is early 1948. Should Earl S. Tupper Company develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its polyethylene moulding and airtight closure? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Consumers will adopt airtight polyethylene containers for food storage because they perceive them as a modern convenience and safety improvement, leading to higher purchase intent and willingness to pay.
theories.T2: Consumers will adopt airtight polyethylene containers because they are perceived as a modern convenience and status symbol, leading to higher purchase intent and willingness to pay, especially among households with disposable income.

sources_read.tupper-hof-contract: undated member profile (written after the decision date)
sources_read.tupper-hof-premiums: undated member profile (written after the decision date)

arguments.quote: the company focused on creating products that other companies sold or offered as novelties or premiums: plastic sandwich picks, cigarette cases, and an unbreakable tumbler offered by Tek toothbrushes with the purchase of any toothbrush.
arguments.does_not_show: No prices paid by households, volumes, or demand for airtight food storage; the buyers described are the promoting firms, not consumers. Says nothing about why a household would pay a premium.

justification.learned: Sources read: tupper-hof-contract, tupper-hof-premiums, tupper-patent-uses. All three describe the company's own contract work, products or its own patent filing. T1 and T2 rest on the same cause (consumer appetite for modern convenience/status) and neither has independent evidence. tupper-hof-premiums adds that Tupper's consumer-facing output was sandwich picks, cigarette cases and a Tek toothbrush tumbler: "novelties or premiums" sold or given away by other firms, not a branded retail line.
justification.uncertain: Whether any household in 1948 paid a premium for airtight polyethylene food storage is unknown: no source read shows a purchase, a price, repeat use or retailer stocking. Unknown too is whether Tupper had any branded retail presence at all, and what glass or metal containers cost. T1 and T2 are near-identical causes, so nothing yet separates them (see tupper-patent-uses, which lists possible uses but no demand).
justification.why_next: Weigh tupper-hof-premiums against T2 as third-party market_fact, because both theories still rest only on company-derived material. It shows a premium/novelty channel to households existed but ran through other firms' promotions, so it speaks to route and value capture rather than household willingness to pay. Next: a third theory with a genuinely different cause (value captured by supplying other brands' premium promotions, not by consumer pricing) plus a non-company source on 1940s kitchen behaviour.

examples.question: Should SIGVARIS GROUP develop a differentiated proposition for people who buy compression without a prescription, such as travellers or athletes, or keep its focus on medical compression? What evidence would justify either choice?

theories.T1: Health-conscious consumers will adopt compression socks for non-medical purposes (travel, daily wear) because they perceive them as a health benefit, leading to higher willingness to pay and repeat purchases.
theories.T2: Athletes will adopt compression socks for non-medical performance benefits because they seek a competitive advantage, leading to higher purchase frequency and willingness to pay premium prices.

arguments.quote: I have worn compression socks while traveling for years but never more than that, even though I should have been wearing them daily. Every sock I tried was always scratchy and uncomfortable.
arguments.does_not_show: It does not show she lacked a prescription (she implies a daily medical need), what she paid, or whether she repurchased; one curated testimonial cannot size a segment or prove willingness to pay.

justification.learned: Seven sources on file, none measuring non-prescription demand. T1 (health framing) and T2 (performance framing) rest on company material: sigvaris-travel-claim asserts DVT risk on flights over four hours; sigvaris-medical-grade-worth says cheaper online products are 'not at all' equivalent; sigvaris-about shows 8 country subsidiaries and 70+ distributor markets but not individual versus prescription share. sigvaris-mordor-cost and sigvaris-mordor-channels give structure (pharmacies 46.5% of revenue, online DTC 11.5% CAGR), not why travellers buy. sigvaris-review-travel is the only customer voice: it shows wearing behaviour, not a company claim.
justification.uncertain: Whether the reviewer in sigvaris-review-travel is a non-prescription buyer at all: 'even though I should have been wearing them daily' suggests a medical indication, so her travel use may be patient behaviour, not the segment T1 describes. Unknown: price paid, repeat purchase, channel, and whether the company curated the testimonial. No source shows purchase frequency, willingness to pay or traveller segment size, so demand is unmeasured.
justification.why_next: Weigh sigvaris-review-travel against T1 (I will assess it on T1, not T2). The quote documents a real behaviour — years of wearing compression socks when travelling — which is stronger than a stated intention, but it also flags discomfort as the recurring barrier and hints the wearer had a medical reason, which is exactly the ambiguity T1 needs resolved. After this assessment the honest next step is to challenge T1 against a non-company source: sigvaris-mordor-cost shows consumers outside the US already self-fund medical compression and that cheaper retail versions undercut validated pressure, which bears on T1's premium value-capture claim. Then a purchase-based test can separate T1 from T2.

examples.question: It is early 1978. Should 3M develop a differentiated proposition for individual buyers, for a specific use case, built on its low-tack repositionable adhesive? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Office workers will adopt repositionable notes because they need temporary, removable notes for brainstorming and collaboration, and will purchase them through standard office supply channels.
theories.T2: DIY enthusiasts and home improvement professionals will adopt repositionable notes because they need temporary, removable labels for projects, and will purchase them through hardware or specialty stores.

arguments.quote: The tacky microspheres provide a pressure-sensitive adhesive which has a low degree of adhesion permitting separation, repositioning and rebonding of adhered objects.
arguments.does_not_show: No DIY user, hardware retailer or purchase appears; it shows the adhesive can be repositioned, not that home improvers would buy, at what price, through which store, or more than once.

justification.learned: From 3m-patent-reposition (1972 patent): the low-tack adhesive is real and permits "separation, repositioning and rebonding" - capability, not demand. From 3m-ee-adhesive (company/teaching claim): the adhesive dates to 1968, no buyer mentioned. From 3m-ap-tomarket (AP, 2021, retrospective): a "Press 'n' Peel memo pad" existed 1974, reached market 1977 - an office use case, dated after the decision point only by a later retelling. examples.question: It is late 2012. Should Cree, Inc. develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its high-brightness LED chips and LED lighting technology? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Consumers will adopt LED bulbs if they are priced low enough to be competitive with incandescent bulbs, because price is the primary barrier to switching.
theories.T2: Consumers will adopt LED bulbs if they perceive them as a premium product offering superior color quality and design, because they value aesthetic and functional differentiation.

arguments.quote: According to retailers, consumers are embracing LEDs, which were the focus of the prize, and CFLs, or compact fluorescent lights, faster than many in the industry expected.
arguments.does_not_show: Second-hand retailer adoption pace, with no prices paid and no reason given; it cannot show whether price or colour quality drove choice. T1 and T2 predict alike, so neither is distinguished.

justification.learned: Cree was not purely B2B before the decision date: cree-pr-ecosmart (company_claim, 2010) shows an EcoSmart downlight sold through The Home Depot at 'less than $50', so a retail channel to individual buyers existed. cree-ledp-reason (company_claim, 2013) has Cree saying it 'needed to give them a reason to switch' — the origin of T1's price-barrier mechanism, but the company describing itself. cree-wiki-first (market_fact) records Cree's 'first consumer products, two household LED bulbs' qualifying for Energy Star in 2013, after the decision date. So T1 and T2 rest only on Cree's own words; no source read shows what buyers did, so demand is unknown.
justification.uncertain: Whether price is the binding constraint (T1) or whether colour quality/design and premium positioning drive switching (T2) — nothing read yet measures either. Also unresolved: the actual 2012 retail prices consumers faced, unit volumes, and whether Home Depot placement produced sales; cree-ledp-reason and cree-wiki-first are both dated after the late-2012 decision point, so they cannot be used as knowable-at-the-time evidence.
justification.why_next: I will weigh cree-bdn-embracing, the only third-party report of consumer behaviour among the sources read, because T1 so far leans on Cree's own claims (cree-ledp-reason, cree-pr-ecosmart) and an outside report is needed to test it. The excerpt reports the pace of adoption but gives no reason for it, so I expect it to leave T1's price mechanism unresolved rather than confirm it — which is the honest result and argues that only a price-ladder test, not more desk reading, can separate T1 from T2.

examples.question: It is 1983. Should Mag Instrument develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its machined anodized-aluminium flashlights? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition because they need reliable, high‑performance flashlights for outdoor recreation and home safety, and they are willing to pay a premium for durability and professional‑grade features.

examples.question: It is late 2009. Should Martek Biosciences develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its algae-derived DHA omega-3 oil? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Health-conscious consumers will adopt a differentiated DHA supplement if they perceive it as a safe, algae-based alternative to fish oil, because they avoid fish allergies and want a sustainable source.
theories.T2: Parents will adopt a differentiated DHA supplement for their children if they perceive it as a safe, mercury‑free alternative to fish oil, because they want to avoid fish allergies and ensure nutritional safety.

arguments.does_not_show: No volumes, revenue, margin, repeat purchase or share taken from fish oil; it shows a consumer product existed and a channel was feasible, not why anyone bought it or what they paid.
arguments.quote: The company also started selling DHA dietary supplements, under the name Neuromins, to supplement diets low in foods that contain DHA.

justification.learned: Established from read sources: Martek is overwhelmingly a B2B ingredient supplier — infant-formula DHA/ARA was 91% of sales in 2007 and 2009 (martek-mw-91pct), its oils are in >99% of US infant formulas (martek-ni10-99pct), and it holds long supply agreements with General Mills and Kellogg (martek-fpw-alliances). examples.question: Should Hilti develop a differentiated proposition for home users or hobbyists, beyond its existing professional offering, or leave that market alone? What evidence would justify either choice?

theories.T1: Homeowners and hobbyists will adopt Hilti tools if they perceive them as reliable and professional-grade, and are willing to pay a premium for durability.
theories.T2: Homeowners and hobbyists will adopt Hilti tools if they perceive them as reliable and professional-grade, and are willing to pay a premium for durability, but will also be sensitive to price and seek the best value.

sources_read.hilti-consumer-market-size: unknown (written while the COVID-19 pandemic was ongoing)

arguments.does_not_show: It is market-level commentary, not Hilti-specific: it does not show Hilti's own consumer demand, how hobbyists differ from average DIY buyers, or what premium, if any, a home user would pay for Hilti specifically.
arguments.quote: Unlike professionals, however – who are generally more willing to pay a premium for better performing and longer lasting power tools – most consumers are very price sensitive when it comes to these products, often opting for less costly imports over expensive professional-grade models.

justification.learned: Hilti is built for business buyers: it runs a direct sales model with ~15,000 people working with customers directly (hilti-direct-model) and per ToolGuyd it "hasn't done much to reach individual end users" (hilti-b2b-reach). The consumer outlet is real but smaller: "about half the size of the professional market" (hilti-consumer-market-size), and 70% of power tool purchasers are homeowners (hilti-homeowners-share), with 70% of purchases in-store and price the top retailer driver (hilti-price-driver). What was missing is any evidence on whether home users would pay a premium, which is the load-bearing assumption of T1.
justification.uncertain: No source read measures Hilti awareness, purchase or willingness to pay among home users; the dossier has no data split by customer type. The price-sensitivity finding (hilti-consumers-price-sensitive) is market-level, so it cannot show Hilti's own consumer demand, and it leaves open the hobbyist sub-segment, which may behave unlike the average DIY buyer. One challenge search remains, plus unread results (hilti-downscale-dilution, hilti-hd-exit).
justification.why_next: T1's mechanism is that professional-grade reliability justifies a premium to home users, but it currently rests on a company claim about capability (hilti-direct-model) and a market-size figure (hilti-consumer-market-size), neither of which addresses willingness to pay. The Freedonia passage (hilti-consumers-price-sensitive) is the only source that speaks directly to that assumption, so weighing it against T1 is the necessary next step before any test or position is defensible.

examples.question: Should ARRI develop a differentiated proposition of its own for individual creators, beyond its professional cinema range and its smartphone partnership, or keep its consumer presence to partners? What evidence would justify either choice?

theories.T1: Individual creators will adopt ARRI products if they perceive them as a status symbol and a differentiator for their work, leading to higher purchase intent and willingness to pay.
theories.T2: Individual creators will adopt ARRI products if they perceive them as a necessary tool for their craft, leading to higher purchase intent and willingness to pay when priced competitively.

arguments.quote: For most filmmakers, ARRI has always been a brand they use rather than a brand they own. ALEXA cameras sit at the top of the professional cinema market, commonly purchased by rental houses, studios, and production companies rather than individual creators.
arguments.does_not_show: It gives no price, no willingness to pay and no test of whether cheaper ARRI gear would convert users into individual buyers; it describes the current purchase channel only, not future demand.

justification.learned: Five sources are read. ARRI's own words keep it anchored to the top end: its 'core focus will continue to be the high-end cinema and live entertainment markets' (arri-core-focus), its newest cinema body is a $55,000 Alexa 35 Xtreme (arri-alexa-price), and its only stated consumer-facing move is imaging software inside a partner's phone (arri-honor-milestone). Nothing read shows individual-creator demand, purchase intent or willingness to pay; the brief says ARRI's finances are not public, so value capture cannot be sized. The two open theories (T1 status, T2 necessary tool) both presume individual creators buy, so the purchase channel is the pivotal factual question.

examples.question: It is late 2012. Should Cree, Inc. develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its high-brightness LED chips and LED lighting technology? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Consumers will adopt LED bulbs if they are priced low enough to be competitive with incandescent bulbs, because price is the primary barrier to switching.
theories.T2: Consumers will adopt LED bulbs if they perceive them as a premium product offering superior color quality and design, because they value aesthetic and functional differentiation.

arguments.quote: According to retailers, consumers are embracing LEDs, which were the focus of the prize, and CFLs, or compact fluorescent lights, faster than many in the industry expected.
arguments.does_not_show: It reports retailers' impression of adoption pace, not why buyers switched; no price comparison, and the same story's 'costly price tag' framing means adoption at high prices cannot be read as proof that price is the primary barrier.

justification.learned: So far: Cree is a B2B chip/component and commercial-fixture maker that had already reached consumers indirectly — an EcoSmart LED downlight at The Home Depot for "less than $50" (cree-pr-ecosmart, company_assertion) — and by the 2012 decision date its own-brand household bulbs were not yet launched (cree-wiki-first). T1 (price is the primary barrier) and T2 (premium colour/design drives switching) rested mainly on Cree's own words (cree-ledp-reason), where an executive says "we needed to give them a reason to switch" without saying what reason. cree-bdn-embracing was read but never weighed; that gap is what I close, since T1's claim about consumers cannot be scored on company claims alone.
justification.uncertain: Whether price or perceived quality is the operative switch trigger: no customer-observation or independent study in the dossier yet measures either. cree-bdn-embracing reports retailer sentiment through a journalist (market_fact), so it establishes adoption momentum, not cause. cree-wiki-first is a 2013-era encyclopedia entry and cannot tell us what was knowable in late 2012. Demand for any differentiated Cree consumer proposition remains unknown, and no financial data was found.
justification.why_next: Weighing cree-bdn-embracing against T1 is the cheapest honest move: it is the one source not from the company that speaks to consumer behaviour at all. If it merely shows adoption without isolating price, T1 stays unsupported beyond company claims, and the next step should be to assess a second, differently-sourced item against T2 and then use the kept challenge on T1's price-primary mechanism.

examples.question: It is late 2009. Should Martek Biosciences develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its algae-derived DHA omega-3 oil? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Health-conscious consumers will adopt a differentiated DHA supplement if they perceive it as a safe, algae-based alternative to fish oil, because they avoid fish allergies and want a sustainable source.
theories.T2: Parents will adopt a differentiated DHA supplement for their children if they perceive it as a safe, algae-based alternative that reduces exposure to fish oil contaminants, because they prioritize child health and safety.

arguments.quote: The company also started selling DHA dietary supplements, under the name Neuromins, to supplement diets low in foods that contain DHA.
arguments.does_not_show: It does not show why anyone bought Neuromins — fish allergy, sustainability or simply a low-DHA diet — nor price, volumes or whether the brand still sold in 2009. A product's existence is not evidence of demand or of the motive T1 names.

justification.learned: Learned: Martek's money is overwhelmingly B2B — 'supplements for infant formula accounted for 91% of the company's sales' in 2007 and 2009 (martek-mw-91pct) — and its DHA reaches shoppers inside other firms' brands, via supply agreements with General Mills and Kellogg (martek-fpw-alliances). Only martek-rfb-neuromins speaks to a Martek-branded consumer proposition. I weigh it on T1 because it is a third-party company history (market_fact), not a Martek release, and T1's premise is that a differentiated algae-DHA proposition for individual buyers is worth building. It adds that such a route already exists: a branded supplement, Neuromins, sold on low-DHA diets, not on fish avoidance.
justification.uncertain: Whether any demand evidence exists for T1 or T2 at all. Both rest on untested motives — fish allergy/sustainability for T1, child safety for T2 — and the dossier holds no customer observation and no independent study; searches_left is 0. Unknown for martek-rfb-neuromins: whether Neuromins was still sold at scale in late 2009, at what price, through which channel, and whether it was ever positioned as fish-free or sustainable. Financial detail is absent from the dossier.
justification.why_next: Weigh martek-rfb-neuromins on T1 now (neutral: capability and existence, not motive), then move to the rival mechanism by assessing martek-mw-91pct against T2: if 91% of sales come from formula makers buying on contract, a parents' child-safety pull is not the lever that moves Martek's revenue. Then spend the one kept challenge on T1's fish-avoidance claim using martek-ni09-infant and martek-fif-awareness, which are company/infant-formula side and cannot establish consumer motive. This assessment of martek-rfb-neuromins changes nothing yet, so T1 stays open.

examples.question: It is early 2014. Should HRA Pharma develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its ulipristal acetate emergency contraceptive? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Women will adopt a consumer-branded emergency contraceptive if they view it as a private, discreet health product, leading to higher purchase intent and willingness to pay.
theories.T2: Women will adopt a consumer-branded emergency contraceptive if they perceive it as a medical necessity, leading to higher purchase intent and willingness to pay.

arguments.quote: Levonorgestrel-containing emergency contraceptives are already available without prescription in most EU countries and are registered for use up to 72 hours after unprotected intercourse or contraceptive failure.
arguments.does_not_show: Regulator's account of licensing for levonorgestrel (not ulipristal) in most EU countries; no data on what women bought, wanted or paid, and no test of medical framing, so it cannot support or refute T2's mechanism.

justification.learned: The demand side is thin. T1 rests only on hra-bmj-3m, a company assertion about 3 million users: volume at most, nothing on discretion or branding; hra-pbr-pioneer is likewise HRA self-description. The non-company items, hra-pbr-ireland and hra-emp-lng, show the channel is not new: NorLevo was "dispensed directly to women in Irish pharmacies" and LNG EC was already non-prescription in most EU countries. What was missing is evidence on T2's mechanism. hra-emp-lng is the right source to weigh on T2 because it comes from the regulator, not the company.
justification.uncertain: Whether either theory has real demand behind it: no source read measures purchase intent, WTP, or repeat purchase for any EC format. hra-emp-lng is dated 2014-11-21, after the early-2014 decision point, so it is usable only for the state of the market it describes, not as a 2014 signal. It also concerns levonorgestrel, not ulipristal, so nothing here establishes how women treat ellaOne specifically. T2 currently has zero direct evidence.
justification.why_next: Because T2 has no evidence at all and T1 rests on company claims, the most honest first step is to record how the one independent-of-company source, hra-emp-lng (EMA/710568/2014), bears on T2. Its quoted sentence describes regulatory status and existing non-prescription availability of a different molecule; it reports no customer behaviour, intent or response to medical framing, so it neither supports nor contradicts T2's purchase-intent claim. Recording it as neutral keeps T2 labelled unevidenced rather than falsely shored up, and flags that a prescription-endorsement proposition is being considered in a market where EC is already largely non-prescription.

examples.question: It is 2014. Should Grundéns develop a differentiated proposition for recreational anglers, building on its commercial fishing raingear? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Recreational anglers will adopt Grundéns raingear because they value durability and professional-grade performance, and they are willing to pay a premium for gear that keeps them dry and comfortable during extended fishing sessions.
theories.T2: Recreational anglers will adopt Grundéns raingear because they value brand recognition and the perceived prestige of using a professional‑grade fishing brand, and they are willing to pay a premium for that association.

arguments.quote: While 9.1 million people stopped fishing, 9.4 million started.
arguments.does_not_show: No spend, price or brand data; it cannot show how many of the entrants stay, or whether the stable core is the premium-paying serious anglers T1 needs. Undated, so 2014 availability is unconfirmed.

justification.learned: T1 and T2 still rest on Grundéns' own voice: grundens-oia-commitment and grundens-sgb-versatility ('versatility and utility make them great for recreational fishing') are company_assertions about products and positioning, not evidence that anglers pay. grundens-nf-herkules is trade press describing Herkules 16 bibs as built to keep commercial fishermen dry — capability, not customer behaviour. grundens-tot-channel is dated 2016, after the 2014 decision date, so unusable. grundens-wiki-churn is the only source on what recreational participants actually do.
justification.uncertain: Whether the churn figure in grundens-wiki-churn is US data, and from which year — the entry is undated, so I cannot confirm it was knowable in 2014. I also do not know the size of the serious, high-spend core within that churn, which is the segment T1 depends on. No source yet shows any purchase, price point or repeat use by a recreational angler, so demand is unknown.
justification.why_next: Before moving toward a position I must weigh the one source that speaks to angler behaviour rather than company intent. I will assess grundens-wiki-churn against T1, because T1's mechanism requires recreational anglers to be durability-driven, premium-paying, repeat buyers; a high-churn participation base of new and lapsing anglers could undercut that. Assessing it against T1 rather than T2 keeps the test honest: T2's prestige mechanism predicts that even short-tenure anglers seek brand signalling, a different observable.

examples.question: It is the mid-1970s. Should Nalge Company develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its plastic laboratory bottles? What evidence would justify that investment?

arguments.claim: Serious outdoor users (backpackers, climbers) buy a bottle mainly to avoid failure in the field: a cracked or leaking container ruins a trip where resupply is impossible. Lab-grade hard polyethylene survives drops and boiling water that break glass, so this group will pay a premium over generic bottles for a guaranteed leak-proof wide-mouth bottle, and replace lost ones.
assumptions: Failure cost, not fashion, drives purchase in this segment.
Lab-grade polyethylene's toughness is a real, demonstrable advantage over glass and cheap plastic.
Specialist outdoor retail exists and can be reached within a modest budget.
A separate consumer brand can be run without cannibalising laboratory sales.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Sell the bottle under a distinct consumer brand at a premium price through specialist outdoor retailers, keeping the higher margin and the credibility of laboratory-grade materials as the proof of reliability.
predictions: Serious multi-day backpackers pay a premium (a stated multiple over generic bottles) for a guaranteed leak-proof bottle, while casual day users do not.
Demand concentrates in specialist outdoor shops and club/mail-order channels, not general hardware or drugstores.
Purchases repeat after loss or wear, and buyers name reliability rather than taste or status as the reason.
A visibly weaker generic bottle at a lower price loses share in this segment when both are shown side by side.
arguments.who_benefits: Backpackers and mountaineers on multi-day trips far from resupply; specialist outdoor retailers who gain a high-margin, credible technical item that pulls traffic.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Once failure has a high cost (lost water, soaked gear, abandoned trip), buyers stop shopping on lowest price and start shopping on proven reliability, so they switch from cheap bottles and canteens to one whose failure mode is known.

justification.learned: `nalgene-outside-mid70s` reports that in the mid-1970s Nalge's own scientists "began sneaking bottles out of headquarters for camping trips" — observed behaviour inside the decision window, but only for employees, not paying outsiders. `nalgene-kelly-division` shows a separate Outdoor Products (consumer) division later carried the classic 32 oz bottle, yet it is a 2020 retrospective: it shows separate consumer organisation was possible, not that 1970s buyers would pay. `nalgene-lab-resin` is a company claim about lab-grade resin — feasibility, not demand. Four sources (nalgene-kelly-patagonia, nalgene-midd-sold, nalgene-wiki-cans, nalgene-wiki-lore) are unread.
justification.uncertain: Whether any non-employee buyer paid for such a bottle before the mid-1970s; whether specialist outdoor retail existed at a scale to reach them; whether a premium could cover a separate consumer channel; whether the driver is failure-avoidance (durability) or purity (no plastic taste/contamination). Retail searches returned nothing usable, so route to buyers and willingness to pay are unknown. No financial data in the dossier.
justification.why_next: The gate is theories: 0 of 2 exist, so no evidence can yet be weighed. I add T1, a failure-avoidance mechanism grounded in the camping behaviour reported in `nalgene-outside-mid70s`, which makes a measurable prediction (serious backpackers pay a premium for a break/leak-proof bottle sold through specialist shops) that a purity-driven rival would not make. Later I can spend the kept-for-challenge search on T1 and read `nalgene-kelly-patagonia` and `nalgene-wiki-cans` to test the channel and competitor assumptions.

examples.question: Should Festool develop a differentiated proposition for hobbyist woodworkers, beyond its existing offering, or keep a single range for all buyers? What evidence would justify either choice?

arguments.claim: Hobbyists buy into an interoperable system, not a cheap tool: the cause of a home-shop woodworker's purchase is that each new tool shares rails, hoses and cases with the next, and that a nearby dealer lets them try it first. A stripped-down cheaper line breaks that mechanism rather than widening the segment.
arguments.who_benefits: Home-shop hobbyists with limited space and no fixed dust installation; Festool and its hobbyist-oriented dealers who sell extractors, hoses, rails and cases alongside each tool.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: A hobbyist who already owns one tool in the system faces real switching cost and gains real utility from a second compatible tool, so they pay premium prices and repeat rather than trading down.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Through system attach: extractors, accessories, consumables and repeat tool purchases at premium price, sold through demonstrator dealers rather than on entry price.
assumptions: Hobbyists are repeat buyers, not one-tool buyers.
Compatibility and dust extraction matter more to a home shop than to a site carpenter.
Festool's 2015 mix shift to professionals reflects professional growth, not hobbyist rejection.
predictions: Hobbyists who enter with a tool plus extractor buy a further compatible tool within 24 months more often than those who enter with a bare tool.
Offering a cheaper non-compatible hobbyist line lowers average revenue per hobbyist and raises one-tool-then-exit buyers.
In a test, hobbyists shown system compatibility (dust extraction, case stacking) convert to purchase at a higher rate than hobbyists shown a lower price.

justification.learned: The three sources read (festool-hobby-growth, festool-mix, festool-woodcraft-origin) are all one 2015 Core77 interview. Festool's own estimate: buyer mix moved from ~70% hobbyist/30% professional in 2004-05 to ~60% professional/40% hobbyist by 2015, and hobbyist growth now lags professional growth. Early hobbyist draw is attributed to very limited distribution plus one large hobbyist-oriented dealer (Woodcraft). So Festool already reaches individual hobbyists at scale through dealer retail; nothing read shows why they buy, what they pay, or whether a differentiated line is wanted.
justification.uncertain: Whether the hobbyist mechanism is price, system compatibility, or dealer access/demonstration. The state has 0 of 2 theories, so no evidence has been assessed against any claim, and no source read so far reports hobbyist spending, willingness to pay, or the size of unmet hobbyist demand.

I add T1 from festool-woodcraft-origin and festool-mix: hobbyists enter via dealer access and stay because tools interoperate, so value sits in the system, not a cheaper tool. Two searches remain, one kept for challenge_theory against T1.

examples.question: It is mid-2015. Should Illumina develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its DNA sequencing and genotyping technology? What evidence would justify that investment?

assumptions: Consumers will not pay for raw genomic data on its own
Third parties can build consumer applications faster and cheaper than Illumina
Illumina can set per-sample prices low enough for partners to run viable consumer products
Privacy and regulatory burden for consumer claims sits mainly with partners
arguments.claim: Illumina's sequencing and array technology is a general-purpose platform whose consumer value lives in applications it does not own. Where third-party developers supply the use-case content and consumer brands bring the customers, adoption occurs without Illumina carrying consumer marketing or brand risk, and Illumina earns per sample from many partners rather than per kit from one own-brand product.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Per-sample sequencing and database fees charged to partners, plus an equity stake in the platform, instead of own-brand consumer margins and consumer acquisition spend.
predictions: Within about a year a partner platform carries several distinct consumer applications, each answering a named question
Partner-attributed sample volume rises while Illumina's own consumer marketing spend stays small
Stated willingness to pay is concentrated on a named use case, not on data volume
arguments.who_benefits: Illumina, from per-sample sequencing demand across many partners; app developers, who avoid building labs and capital cost; consumer brands, who add a DNA feature to an existing audience.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Individuals pay only when a specific question (ancestry, family matching, fitness) is answered cheaply; partners supply that answer, so the buyer never has to value raw genomic data.
