examples.question: It is mid-1991. Should Diatek Corporation develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its infrared ear thermometer for hospitals? What evidence would justify that investment?

sources_read.diatek-spinoff-device: 1991 (originally published; note on later acquisition added afterwards)

assumptions: Probe thermometers require a minute or more of stillness, so readings on young children frequently fail or are refused.
The measured group already owns a thermometer and treats a second purchase as replacing a failing tool.
Diatek's ear accuracy is accepted by paediatricians by 1991, so endorsement is obtainable.
Retail distribution can be reached without ceding all margin to a distributor.
arguments.claim: The binding constraint on home temperature-taking is the child's cooperation, not price. A sleeping or resisting child cannot hold a probe still for the minutes it needs, so carers fail when they most need a reading. A two-second ear reading removes that failure, so households replace their probe thermometer and a maker owning sensor and calibration holds a premium.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Premium unit price plus repeat purchase (second device, probe covers) through paediatrician endorsement and pharmacy shelves; margin rests on sensor/calibration know-how and clinical credibility, not advertising.
predictions: Among households with a child under five, the share buying a dedicated ear unit within 12 months exceeds the share buying any new probe thermometer.
Stated willingness to pay for the ear device exceeds the price of the best-selling probe thermometer by at least a third, and deposit/purchase conversion holds at that premium.
Repeat use, not first purchase, is high: most buyers report using it more than once a month during illness season.
arguments.who_benefits: Parents and carers of children under about five, plus night-time carers who must read temperature without waking the child; they get a reading that currently fails.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: The two-second, non-contact eardrum reading converts a failed, distressing task into a completed one, so the household substitutes a new device for the probe thermometer it already owns rather than adding a marginal gadget.

justification.learned: Sources read: diatek-jpl-market, diatek-jpl-tap, diatek-spinoff-device. Together they show capability and medical positioning only: Model 7000 launched 1991 as a "pioneering effort to modify space-based infrared sensors for a medical infrared thermometer" (diatek-jpl-market), eight ounces and under two seconds via eardrum IR (diatek-spinoff-device), built with late-1980s JPL TAP help (diatek-jpl-tap). No source shows any individual buyer, consumer channel, retail price, unit volumes or demand. Who currently buys Diatek's thermometers, and at what price, is unknown. Two dossier results remain unread: diatek-patent-rival, diatek-pm-zones.
justification.uncertain: Whether Diatek sells to any individual buyers at all, and through what channel (hospital distributor, pharmacy, mail order) - none of diatek-jpl-market, diatek-jpl-tap, diatek-spinoff-device addresses this. Whether parents of young children would pay a premium over existing glass/mercury or probe thermometers in 1991. What diatek-patent-rival and diatek-pm-zones contain. No financial or price data exists in the dossier.
justification.why_next: Stage requires at least 2 theories and I have 0; repeat searches are refused. So I add T1 now, a causal mechanism drawn from the reading-speed and non-contact properties documented in diatek-spinoff-device: the group that gains most is parents of sleeping or uncooperative children, who today cannot get a reading without waking or restraining the child. Next, read the unread diatek-patent-rival to ground a genuinely different rival cause (patent/competitor dynamics) rather than inventing one, then add T2.

examples.question: It is late 2014. Should Perrigo develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its over-the-counter medicine development and manufacturing? What evidence would justify that investment?

arguments.claim: In European OTC categories, shoppers buy the brand name they recognise, not the factory behind it. A manufacturer with no consumer franchise therefore captures little value from a new proposition unless it owns a locally trusted brand, so Perrigo's route to consumer premiums is acquiring or building named brands (as with Omega's Abtei, Lactacyd, Solpadeine) rather than putting 'Perrigo' on the pack.
arguments.who_benefits: Owners of locally recognised OTC brand names, and manufacturers able to buy them at a discount to the premium stream they generate - not contract manufacturers selling unbadged output.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Shoppers facing a symptom with uncertain outcome use brand familiarity as a quality proxy; a name they do not know is read as risk, so they pay a premium or default to the familiar pack.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: By owning the trademark and thus the retail price premium and repeat purchase; manufacturing margin alone is a commodity return negotiated by the brand owner.
assumptions: Shoppers cannot judge OTC quality directly and use brand names as proxies
Brand loyalty survives price gaps up to some threshold, beyond which suspicion sets in
Retailers stock names that shoppers ask for, so brand pull buys shelf space
Perrigo's own corporate name carries little recognition with European shoppers in 2014
predictions: A Perrigo-corporate-branded OTC launched without an acquired local name sells materially less per store than an equivalently priced, locally named brand
Acquired local brands sustain a retail price premium over store-brand equivalents, whereas unbranded manufacturer output does not
Repeat purchase rates are higher for recognised names than for unfamiliar names at identical price and pack

justification.learned: Perrigo already reaches consumers indirectly: store-brand cetirizine hit 48% penetration ([perrigo-bar-penetration], a company claim, not demand proof). It is also buying Omega Pharma, ~$1.6bn revenue, fifth-largest European OTC player with local brands bought from GSK such as Abtei, Lactacyd, Solpadeine ([perrigo-ppr-omega], [perrigo-pml-gsk]). Historical observers say too-large price gaps made consumers suspicious and drove them back to national brands ([perrigo-fu-suspicious]). So consumer-facing assets exist; what is unclear is the mechanism by which a manufacturer captures value from them. No theories exist yet.
justification.uncertain: Whether European shoppers buy OTC on brand trust, pharmacist/retailer recommendation, or price; whether Perrigo could carry a brand itself or only via acquired local names. 48% penetration is a company assertion, not independent demand evidence. Two unread results ([perrigo-fu-goodsense], [perrigo-ppr-pharmacies]) may bear on pharmacy channel power. No financials in the dossier.

justification.learned: Three sources read. examples.question: Should ARRI develop a differentiated proposition of its own for individual creators, beyond its professional cinema range and its smartphone partnership, or keep its consumer presence to partners? What evidence would justify either choice?

arguments.claim: Individual creators value ARRI's image science (colour, look, on-set-to-post pipeline) more than they value owning ARRI hardware. If that look can be delivered inside tools they already own — phones, editing/colour software, third-party rigs — they will pay a premium for the ARRI badge, so ARRI captures value by licensing its image science rather than by selling cameras to individuals.
arguments.who_benefits: Individual creators and small teams who need client-credible professional image quality without a $55,000 camera body or a rental booking.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: They pick a phone or software tool carrying ARRI image science over a cheaper rival because the look arrives closer to final, cuts grading time, and signals professionalism to paying clients.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Per-device or per-seat licensing fees from manufacturers such as HONOR plus possible software subscription; near-zero marginal hardware cost and no new direct retail channel.
assumptions: ARRI's look is recognisable and valued by buyers outside professional cinema.
Device makers and app vendors will pay for the badge and image pipeline.
Purchases by individual creators are swayed by colour-science and pipeline claims, not only price and specs.
Licensing a partner does not erode ARRI's professional positioning or rental demand.
predictions: In a price-choice test, individual creators choose an ARRI-badged phone/app over an equally specced unbranded one at a 10-20% higher price, while a control group with no branding does not.
Creators who adopt ARRI-licensed mobile/software tools keep renting or buying ARRI cinema gear at similar rates, i.e. no cannibalisation.
Additional device makers approach ARRI for image-science licensing after the HONOR launch is publicised.

justification.learned: From arri-ymc-use-not-own: ARRI is "a brand they use rather than a brand they own"; ALEXA is "commonly purchased by rental houses, studios, and production companies rather than individual creators", so individual access runs through rental, not purchase. arri-alexa-price: the new Alexa 35 Xtreme lists at $55,000, and owners are considering selling amid a difficult cinema market. arri-honor-milestone: ARRI calls the HONOR Robot Phone "an important milestone in ARRI's expansion into Content Creation" giving "more creators access". So ARRI's only evidenced individual route is partner licensing, and no source yet shows individual willingness to pay.
justification.uncertain: Whether individual creators actually value the ARRI look enough to pay for it, and how much: no source read shows individual purchasing behaviour, price sensitivity or demand. Unread results arri-cined-challenges and arri-core-focus may bear on the professional/rental side, which I have not yet weighed. ARRI's finances and licence terms with HONOR are unknown, so value capture per unit is unknown.
justification.why_next: Stage requires 2+ theories and there are none, so nothing can be assessed, challenged or tested. My call adds the first mechanism (returned as T1): creators buy the ARRI look, not ARRI hardware, so licensing image science to devices/apps captures value. It rests on arri-honor-milestone and arri-ymc-use-not-own, and its predictions (premium willingness to pay for ARRI-badged mobile/software tools, no camera cannibalisation) differ from a rival rental-market theory, which I will add next using arri-core-focus and arri-cined-challenges.

examples.question: Should ARRI develop a differentiated proposition of its own for individual creators, beyond its professional cinema range and its smartphone partnership, or keep its consumer presence to partners? What evidence would justify either choice?

arguments.claim: Individual creators treat a cinema camera as a per-project cost, not an asset: they rent or borrow rather than buy. Their spending is therefore bounded by single-project budgets, so a maker that sells access - rental, subscription, or imaging software embedded in a tool they already own like a smartphone - captures more of that spending than one selling a 55,000-dollar body.
arguments.who_benefits: Individual creators and small production outfits whose project income is irregular; rental houses and partners who already own the capital equipment and the customer relationship.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: They adopt a tool only when its cost fits one project's budget or is bundled into a workflow they already pay for, so they switch on access and per-use terms, not on ownership.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Per-use or subscription fees, software/licence royalties and hardware-partner royalties, capturing value without selling capital equipment to buyers who cannot amortise it.
assumptions: Individual creator project budgets are small and irregular relative to 55,000-dollar hardware
Rental or subscription access is a credible substitute for ownership for this group
ARRI can license imaging science through partners without diluting its professional brand
predictions: At a 55,000-dollar purchase price, stated purchase intent among individual creators is near zero while access-based intent is materially higher
Individual demand concentrates in rental, subscription or partner-bundled offerings rather than outright body purchases
Willingness to pay per project or per month exists even where willingness to pay for a body does not

justification.learned: ARRI's read evidence shows a rental-led professional model: newest body is a "$55,000 Alexa 35 Xtreme" (arri-alexa-price); filmmakers see ARRI as "a brand they use rather than a brand they own," with ALEXAs "commonly purchased by rental houses, studios, and production companies rather than individual creators" (arri-ymc-use-not-own). Its only consumer route is partner-based: the HONOR Robot Phone, a company claim of "ARRI's expansion into Content Creation" giving "more creators access" (arri-honor-milestone).
justification.uncertain: No demand evidence at all: no survey, no stated willingness to pay, no individual-buyer sales figure. The HONOR framing is a company assertion, not proof individuals want ARRI-branded tools. Unread results arri-cined-challenges and arri-core-focus may bear on rental-market stress and ARRI's core-focus orientation. Prior calls were refused only because they repeated identical searches/reads.
justification.why_next: The stage blocker is theories: 0 of 2, so no mechanism exists to weigh evidence against. I add T1 on arri-ymc-use-not-own and arri-alexa-price, where individual spending is bounded by per-project budgets, so access models (rental, subscription, embedded software) should out-earn ownership sales of a 55,000-dollar body - a claim a brand-prestige rival will predict against differently.

examples.question: It is spring 2021. Should Sensirion develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its CO2 and environmental sensors? What evidence would justify that investment?

arguments.claim: Individual buyers purchase a room CO2 monitor to resolve a felt problem - stuffy air, poor concentration, ventilation worry - not to own a sensor. If a maker turns the reading into a verdict ('ventilate now'), buying becomes a comfort decision, and whoever owns that interpretation plus the brand sells a finished device at consumer prices, not component margins.
arguments.who_benefits: Households and home-office or child-room occupants who suspect their air is poor but lack an instrument telling them when to act; retailers gain a demo-able category.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: A number plus a verdict converts vague discomfort into a triggered action (open window, move desk), so willingness to pay attaches to the interpretation and its credibility - a trusted sensor brand - rather than to specifications.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Sell a finished branded monitor direct or through retail at a consumer price multiple of the sensor's component price, keeping calibration, algorithm and design in-house rather than handing them to an OEM.
assumptions: Buyers feel an air-quality problem they cannot currently measure
Interpretation, not the sensor, is what they pay for
Sensirion's sensor credibility transfers to a consumer brand
A consumer price point sustains margin above component sales
predictions: At a proposed DTC price of EUR 99-149, conversion is higher on a page showing an actionable verdict than one showing accuracy specs
Owners act on alerts (logged ventilation events) in week 1 and keep using the device beyond week 4
Stated willingness to pay tracks the verdict, not the measurement accuracy claim

justification.learned: Sensirion's consumer exposure is small and mostly indirect: 2020 consumer sales were CHF 14.9m, up 5.3%, and consumer was only 5.9% of revenue versus Medical 44.3%, Industrial 28.1%, Automotive 21.7% (sensirion-ar20-consumer, sensirion-ar20-split). The only consumer-facing artefact in the dossier so far is the SCD4x CO2 Gadget, which the company itself calls a 'demonstrator' for its sensor product line (sensirion-gadget-page) - a component showcase, not a retail product. So what it sells to individual buyers is still unknown.
justification.uncertain: Nothing read yet shows an individual buyer making a purchase, a price point, repeat use, or a use case anyone asked for. sensirion-aivc-austria is read but not yet weighed, and the dossier's financials are company-level only, so no consumer unit economics exist.
justification.why_next: The refusal is correct: searches on the home-air-quality query were repeated three times with no new result, and the stage is 'theories' with 0 of 2, so nothing exists to weigh or test. The right call is add_theory, grounded in sensirion-gadget-page and sensirion-ar20-consumer: a demand-side mechanism for why an individual buyer would pay for a room CO2 monitor (a verdict, not a sensor), which a rival OEM design-win theory can later be tested against.

examples.question: Should Cotral Lab develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing hearing-protection offering? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Professional musicians will adopt custom-moulded hearing protection if it is marketed as a performanceenhancing tool that preserves sound quality while blocking noise, because they value accurate sound and are willing to pay a premium for a product that does not compromise their craft.
theories.T2: Sleep aid users will adopt custom-moulded hearing protection if it is marketed as a medical-grade solution that reduces sleep disruption caused by background noise, because they seek a product that addresses a specific health concern and are willing to pay for a solution that improves sleep quality.

justification.learned: The dossier has real evidence: bockstael-2015-looks (independent test group: appreciation of musician earplugs depended mainly on comfort and looks, sound-quality differences less noticeable) and minuendo-claim (a commercial adjustable high-fidelity musician earplug exists, 7-25dB), plus company claims ctl-3d, ctl-it1, ctl-filter, ctl-onsite, ctl-channel (products distributed mainly direct to end-user companies, not individual consumers). T1 and T2 are both stated; only ctl-it1, ctl-filter, ctl-onsite and ctl-deal have been assessed, all company assertions, none showing demand.
justification.uncertain: Real demand from any consumer group is unknown: no source read shows a purchase of Cotral product by an individual. Whether Cotral reaches individual buyers at all is unknown — ctl-channel suggests business-to-business distribution. T1's mechanism (musicians pay premium for sound preservation) is partly undercut by bockstael-2015-looks (looks and comfort mattered more than sound quality). T2 has only company claims behind it. SYN-C is SIMULATED and cannot bear on either theory.
justification.why_next: The finishes were refused for citing SYN-C, a simulated wear test, as support for a real-demand recommendation, and for a T1 revision that reasoned from SYN-C. I will read it (read_source etymotic-er20xs) so the conclusion rests on real market facts rather than SYN-C, then correct T1's revision and finish without SYN-C.

examples.question: It is late 2017. Should Lenzing AG develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its lyocell and modal fibres? What evidence would justify that investment?

arguments.claim: Lenzing captures value through ingredient branding, not consumer products: apparel brands buy a named, certified fibre to borrow its softness and sustainability story cheaply, so lyocell demand grows while the buying decision stays with brands and mills, and Lenzing earns a fibre-level premium for the trademark.
arguments.who_benefits: Apparel brands and retailers (Inditex/Zara first) that need a credible fibre story cheaply; Lenzing as owner of the Tencel trademark.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Brands specify fibre by trademark because a recognised ingredient transfers trust to a garment at little cost; mills then buy branded lyocell to win those orders.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Premium price on branded lyocell and modal plus co-marketing and downstream specification control; no consumer product or retail channel needed.
assumptions: Consumers recognise and trust the Tencel name at the point of sale
Brands and mills pay more for a named, certifiable fibre than for generic lyocell
Lenzing controls and can enforce the trademark along the chain
predictions: Partner-brand garments carry visible Tencel swing tags or fibre call-outs more often than unbranded-fibre garments in the same stores
Brands offered co-marketing commit to larger year-on-year specified volumes than control brands offered none
A measurable price premium of branded over generic lyocell persists in 2017

justification.learned: Five sources read: lenzing-te2017-lyocell (lyocell demand grew 128% by 2017), lenzing-wiki-tencel1992 (Lenzing bought Tencel in 2000, kept the brand name), lenzing-ar16-zara (Inditex/Zara sells Refibra garments as "strategic partner"), lenzing-hustvedt-organic (53% of two segments used organic-cotton share to decide purchase), lenzing-pefc-labels (label information gap, but 2024, after the decision date). No theory added yet; both refused calls were repeat searches.
justification.uncertain: Whether and how Lenzing reaches individual buyers: licensing, swing tags, co-marketing or own retail. Three results are unread: lenzing-pr18-b2b2c, lenzing-pr18-research, lenzing-wtin-swingtags. Also unknown whether consumers pay a premium for a named fibre from a source dated before late 2017, since lenzing-pefc-labels is 2024.
justification.why_next: Stage is theories with 0 added. T1 states the ingredient-branding mechanism implied by lenzing-te2017-lyocell and lenzing-wiki-tencel1992: Lenzing monetises the Tencel trademark at fibre level by selling to brands, not consumers, so a proposition aimed at individual buyers would be the wrong unit of investment. Next the investigation needs a rival with a different cause, grounded in lenzing-pr18-b2b2c and lenzing-wtin-swingtags.

examples.question: It is 1924. Should Leitz develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its precision optics and a small-format camera that its development head built to test cinema film exposures? What evidence would justify that investment?

arguments.claim: Amateur and outdoor photographers are the group that would change behaviour: they cannot carry a plate camera with tripod into the field, but a hand-held camera taking cheap 35 mm cinema film lets them shoot many exposures cheaply and spontaneously, so they would buy a small-format camera as a personal instrument rather than a laboratory tool.
arguments.who_benefits: Individual amateur and outdoor photographers who want photographs away from a studio and cannot afford or carry large-format plates and tripods.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Per-exposure cost falls and the camera becomes carryable, so a photographer who previously took a few planned plate exposures can now take many opportunistic ones — a change in what they do, not just in what they own.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Leitz sells the whole instrument (body plus its own precision lens) at a premium to individuals, capturing value from optical quality and brand rather than from film or processing.
assumptions: 35 mm cinema film is cheap and widely available to consumers, not only to studios
Hand-held small-format images are acceptable in quality to non-professional buyers
Leitz's precision lens is hard for rivals to match, so buyers pay a premium
A distribution route to individual buyers exists or can be built
predictions: Given the choice, outdoor/amateur photographers take up the small camera at a higher rate than studio, scientific or industrial buyers
Demand is sensitive to body-plus-lens price relative to a plate camera, and buyers cite portability and film cost as reasons
Repeat use is high among amateurs (many exposures per owner) and low among in-house laboratory users

justification.learned: leitz-wpb-preprod: Barnack built 31 pre-production cameras "for the factory and for outdoor photographers"; prototypes got a mixed reception; Leitz decided on production in 1924. leitz-dcw-filmtest: the compact camera originated as an in-house device to check cinema film speed. leitz-lc-resistance: "many managers and engineers were sceptical of series production in 1924." justification.uncertain: Whether individual photographers actually bought, requested or paid a premium for such a camera before 1924 — leitz-phsc-enlarge and leitz-wpl-lens are still unread. Financial and price data absent from the dossier. No theory yet (T-count 0), so no assessment possible.

examples.question: It is early 1978. Should 3M develop a differentiated proposition for individual buyers, for a specific use case, built on its low-tack repositionable adhesive? What evidence would justify that investment?

assumptions: Workers in document-handling roles actually feel clean removal as the binding constraint, not cheap paper or convenience of supply.
Repeat purchase occurs: pads are consumed and reordered, not one-off curiosities.
Adhesive and coating cost is low enough that a branded pad carries a premium over plain paper.
Stationery retail or office-supply distribution can reach these buyers.
No existing low-cost substitute already satisfies clean removal acceptably.
arguments.claim: Office document handling creates recurring moments when a worker must mark or attach something to a page they must not damage. Clean removal, not stickiness, is the binding constraint: a lightly-adhering, residue-free note replaces tape-and-staple improvisation, and buyers pay a premium, sold as a repeat-purchase coated-paper pad, not bulk adhesive.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Sell the consumable — coated paper pads at branded stationery margins through office-supply and stationery channels — instead of licensing or dumping bulk adhesive; the patented microsphere adhesive stays an in-house coated input.
predictions: Offices given free sample pads in a document-heavy workflow will reorder paid pads within roughly 8-12 weeks at a rate well above zero, and reorder rates will exceed those of a matched group given only bulk adhesive and instructions.
When offered a choice, buyers will pay a measurable premium for the removable pad over an equally sticky permanent-note alternative, even at equal sheet count.

Purchase concentrates in document-annotation roles and rarely appears among buyers with no shared-document workflow, which a rival explanation based on general novelty or advertising reach would not predict.
arguments.who_benefits: Clerical and secretarial staff, file clerks, librarians, drafters and engineers who annotate shared or permanent documents they must return undamaged.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Existing fixatives fail the must-not-damage requirement: tape tears fibres, staples perforate, clips slide and mark. A note that adheres lightly and repositions removes the improvisation and the rework cost of a damaged original.

justification.learned: Read: 3m-patent-reposition establishes a genuine capability — a pressure-sensitive adhesive with "a low degree of adhesion permitting separation, repositioning and rebonding" (granted 1972). 3m-ee-adhesive dates the discovery to 1968. 3m-gale-opposition shows only that 3M's "designers and engineers... were convinced the note pads could not be made" — internal manufacturing doubt, which is not customer demand. No source read shows a product reaching a buyer, a price, a channel or a purchase. Theory count is still 0, which is what blocked progress.
justification.uncertain: Whether any product using the adhesive was sold before early 1978, at what price, through which channel (unread: 3m-ap-solution, 3m-ap-tomarket, 3m-mnopedia-mixed, 3m-mnopedia-search). Whether the clean-removal property is worth paying a premium for, or whether buyers substitute free improvisations (tape, clips, torn corners). No financial or cost-of-goods data in the dossier, so margin per pad is unknown.
justification.why_next: Stage is "theories" with 0 of at least 2; nothing further can be weighed or challenged until a mechanism exists. I add T1: the causal claim that temporary document annotation is the recurring job, the clean-removal property is what changes behaviour, and value is captured by selling a branded consumable paper pad rather than bulk adhesive. This is testable against a rival mechanism, and rests only on the capability in 3m-patent-reposition, not on any unproven demand claim.

examples.question: It is late 1974. Should Statitrol Corporation develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its ionization smoke-detection technology? What evidence would justify that investment?

sources_read.statitrol-spr-commercial: 2016 (prize review; written after the decision date)

justification.learned: From statitrol-ieee-aec: AEC approved detectors for commercial properties 1963, residential only 1969. examples.question: It is late 2015. Should Danfoss A/S develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its thermostatic radiator valve and electronic heating-control technology? What evidence would justify that investment?

arguments.claim: Owners of boiler-heated European homes who pay their own heating bills buy per-room electronic TRV heads because they can cut spend in unused rooms without a new boiler, wiring or installer, so retrofit simplicity plus visible savings — not app connectivity — drives purchase.
arguments.who_benefits: Owner-occupier who pays the fuel bill and heats rooms unevenly; Danfoss captures a price premium over a mechanical TRV head.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Room-level setback turns an abstract bill into a controllable per-room saving, and battery-powered screw-on heads let a household act without tradesmen or building works.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Sell the electronic head plus app as a premium-priced accessory through existing wholesaler and retail channels, keeping the mechanical valve body installed base as the retrofit market.
assumptions: Householders in the target segment pay their own heating bill
Battery TRV heads fit existing valve bodies without plumbing work
Savings are large enough to be noticed and attributed within one heating season
Mechanical TRVs in place leave room-level control improvable
predictions: Households quoting a payback under two heating seasons convert at a materially higher rate than those shown features alone
Buyers name bill savings, not app features, as the reason when asked after purchase
Purchasing households buy more than one head, i.e. multi-room baskets rather than single units
Conversion is higher in older, poorly insulated, individually-billed dwellings than in new-build or heat-included rentals

justification.learned: Four sources read. danfoss-eco-30: company claim of "up to 30% savings" and easy install/use. danfoss-prn-zones: in boiler-based European homes, Nest/Tado/Netatmo "do not provide independent control of different heating zones". danfoss-wiki-1943: TRV "promoted as an energy saving device" in 1952. danfoss-prn-cagr (2017, after decision date): 2.75% CAGR. No source read shows direct-to-consumer sales, a price, or homeowner demand.
justification.uncertain: Whether Danfoss reaches individual buyers at all: unread danfoss-php-installer and danfoss-sup-2011 may bear on installer channel and product range. No demand, willingness-to-pay or unit-price evidence found; the 30% saving is a company assertion, not measured.
justification.why_next: Stage is theories, 0 of 2. The refusal blocks repeat price searches (1 search left, 1 kept for challenge). Reading danfoss-prn-zones plus danfoss-eco-30 supports a mechanism about per-zone control and retrofit, so add T1 grounded on those ids rather than search again.

examples.question: Should Sievi develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing safety and occupational footwear offering? What evidence would justify that investment?

arguments.claim: Protective footwear is bought to stop pain, not to satisfy a rule: because standard safety shoes reliably cause discomfort, individual buyers with a real physical exposure (ice, cold, long standing) outside work will pay a premium for a shoe whose comfort and grip are the product's purpose, so a maker can sell its existing safety platform to consumers with no redesign.
arguments.who_benefits: Non-occupational wearers facing winter ice, cold and long standing, plus anyone with foot pain from ordinary work-style shoes; the manufacturer gains a consumer price point on an existing platform.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: They now either tolerate painful safety-style shoes or buy separate anti-slip devices; a shoe that removes the pain and the add-on in one purchase changes what they choose at the shelf.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Premium price per pair over generic winter boots, sold through the consumer channel already stocking the range, with no new tooling and no new factory.
assumptions: Comfort pain is salient enough at the point of purchase to beat a lower price
Individual buyers can identify the Sievi brand in a multi-brand webstore
Ice/cold exposure is frequent enough to justify a specialised pair
Existing studded and anti-slip models already meet the comfort need without redesign
predictions: In a comparable winter offer, the share of non-occupational buyers choosing the comfort/grip model over a cheaper generic boot exceeds 25%
Stated comfort ranks above price when these buyers rank purchase reasons
Repeat purchase or second-pair rate among individual buyers is higher than among one-off occupational buyers

justification.learned: Three sources read. sievi-alix-survey: individual footwear buyers rank quality (91%) and comfort (90%) above price (75%) — a category purchase-driver, not a Sievi fact. sievi-arceri-review: safety footwear consistently produces "symptomatic discomfort and pain" — an unsolved problem in the category, not proof of willingness to pay. sievi-karkkainen: Sievi safety, winter, studded shoes and anti-slip devices are already listed in a third-party consumer webstore, so reach to individual buyers exists, but no volumes, prices or margins are shown. No theory exists yet.
justification.uncertain: Whether the comfort pain documented in sievi-arceri-review applies to non-occupational winter buyers, and whether the assortment listed on sievi-karkkainen sells at a premium or sells at all — the excerpt gives assortment only. No source yet tests the rival mechanism (brand familiarity carried from employer-issued footwear); sievi-yle-employer is unread. Consumer demand size and margin capture remain unknown.
justification.why_next: Stage is theories at 0 of 2, so no assessment or test can proceed. T1 is added now, built directly on the three read sources: sievi-arceri-review supplies the unresolved harm, sievi-alix-survey supplies the stated priority of comfort/quality over price, and sievi-karkkainen supplies the existing consumer channel carrying studded and anti-slip product. T1 must be a mechanism about individual buyers, not advice, so that a rival theory with a different cause (workplace familiarity, or channel/margin capture) can later be tested against it with a discriminating measure.

examples.question: Should Festool develop a differentiated proposition for hobbyist woodworkers, beyond its existing offering, or keep a single range for all buyers? What evidence would justify either choice?

arguments.claim: Hobbyist woodworkers buy Festool as a one-off identity and quality investment in an interoperable system: because tools, cases and dust extraction work together and the brand carries workshop prestige, a high per-tool price reads as rational value rather than a barrier, so a stripped-down 'hobbyist' line would be chosen only rarely when the full system is offered alongside.
arguments.who_benefits: Hobbyists get prestige and a coherent system that retains resale value; Festool captures premium margins plus follow-on accessory and consumable sales within the same ecosystem.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Hobbyists evaluate purchases against ecosystem fit and long-term ownership, not against rival per-tool prices, and each system purchase raises the cost of switching, so they stay inside the range instead of trading down.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Premium pricing on system components, plus repeat accessory, abrasive and consumable sales to buyers already locked into the compatible platform and dealer network.
assumptions: Hobbyists buy few tools but at high unit value.
Compatibility and dust extraction matter more to them than unit price.
Prestige/resale value is part of why they accept the premium.
A cheaper simplified line would be compared against the full range, not only against rival brands.
predictions: When a cheaper simplified hobbyist line is shown beside the full system, fewer than one in three hobbyist buyers chooses the cheaper line.
Hobbyists' repeat spend concentrates in accessories and consumables for tools they already own, not in new lower-priced tool categories.
Stated willingness to pay for guaranteed system compatibility (cases, extraction, hose fit) is high among hobbyists, and price-rank of the main objection falls once compatibility is assured.

justification.learned: From festool-mix, festool-hobby-growth and festool-woodcraft-origin: hobbyists dominated early Festool USA sales (~70/30 hobbyist/pro around 2004-05, ~40/60 by 2015) and were reached via a hobby-oriented dealer (Woodcraft) under deliberately limited distribution; hobbyist growth is now slower than professional. From festool-fww-price, price is the salient objection individual buyers voice ("are they 5 times better than everyone else?"). Sources read: fww-price, hobby-growth, mix, woodcraft-origin.
justification.uncertain: No evidence yet shows WHY hobbyists pay: system/prestige justification versus paying despite price. Nothing read measures hobbyist willingness to pay, repeat purchase, or response to a cheaper line. Unread results festool-bigbox and festool-ukw-overpaid may bear on price and distribution.
justification.why_next: Stage is theories with 0 of 2, and I still hold 1 search for the challenge, so no search is needed yet. I add T1, a premium-justification mechanism grounded in festool-fww-price, festool-mix and festool-woodcraft-origin, so a distinct price-barrier rival (T2) can later be tested against it.

examples.question: It is 1928. Should Carrier Engineering Corporation develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its refrigeration and humidity-control engineering? What evidence would justify that investment?

assumptions: A visible prestige segment of households exists with incomes high enough to buy a system costing many times a room heater
Comfort and status, not running cost, drive the purchase decision for that segment
Carrier can control design and installation quality through a dedicated residential channel
arguments.claim: Cooled, dehumidified indoor air is bought by affluent households as a comfort-and-status good, in the same way they already buy central heating and automobiles. Because such buyers judge the purchase by comfort and standing rather than by cost per degree, they will pay a premium far above what middle-income households would pay for the same cooling.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: A differentiated residential brand (Carrier-Lyle) with Carrier-controlled design, installation standards and dealer network, earning premium equipment and installation margins rather than commodity component sales.
predictions: When offered a branded residential system and a cheaper unbranded equivalent to the same affluent group, a majority choose the branded one at a premium
Stated willingness to pay among affluent households exceeds the installed cost of a typical system, while middle-income households' willingness falls below it
Early residential buyers cluster in high-income districts and own cars and central heating at above-average rates
arguments.who_benefits: Affluent urban and suburban homeowners who already buy prestige comfort goods, and Carrier itself if it owns the branded residential channel rather than selling components.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: A visible, engineered 'Manufactured Weather' system converts an invisible technical service into a displayable marker of modern, healthy living, so these households buy earlier and pay more than a purely utilitarian calculus would justify.

justification.learned: Read three sources. carrier-doe-metropolitan shows Carrier installed a designed cooling system at Los Angeles's Metropolitan Theater in 1922, pumping cool air through high vents for humidity control and comfort — capability in large enclosed spaces, not households. carrier-wc-lyle is Carrier's own retrospective: subsidiary Carrier-Lyle was founded in 1928 "responding to the emerging residential market," promoting "Manufactured Weather in the home" — company intent, not demand. carrier-wc-hesitant concedes Depression-era consumers "were still hesitant to embrace air conditioning," but covers a period after 1928. Feasibility is documented; willingness of individual buyers to pay is not.
justification.uncertain: Whether any real evidence on individual buyers exists in the dossier: seven results are still unread (carrier-achr-300, carrier-ch-1930, carrier-ch-chiller, carrier-doe-flocked, carrier-sim-35, carrier-wic-crash, carrier-wic-depression). Price of a residential system, household incomes, and any actual home sales are unknown; the brief states financial data is absent. Search budget is nearly spent (1 left, 1 kept for challenge), so unread sources carry most of the remaining information value.
justification.why_next: The stage gate requires at least two theories and the dossier has none, so no evidence can yet be weighed. I add T1 as the first mechanism, drawn from carrier-wc-lyle: affluent households treat cooled, dehumidified indoor air as a comfort-and-status good. This gives the surviving search and the kept challenge a target: T1 predicts a small, high-price, prestige buyer segment served through a branded residential channel, whereas a rival mechanism (unit economics making homes unaffordable, or small commercial proprietors as the only paying individual buyers) predicts different buyers and different behaviour on price and repeat purchase.

examples.question: It is 1888. Should S.L. Allen & Co. develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its farm-implement manufacturing? What evidence would justify that investment?

assumptions: Many growers farm plots too small for a standard-width drill
Their current method is hand sowing or borrowing a neighbour's drill
Existing cultivator parts can be combined into a working compact drill
Growers buy tools outright rather than renting
arguments.claim: Small-plot growers - market, truck and estate gardeners - are a distinct buyer group whose plots are too narrow to justify a full-width seed drill. They sow by hand because a standard drill's price and scale do not fit, so a compact drill assembled from the firm's existing cultivator parts (wheels, trusses, levers) would convert them: it replaces hand labour at a price their plot size can repay.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Shared components with the existing cultivator line hold unit cost down; the compact drill sells at a modest premium through the firm's existing implement dealers.
predictions: Among buyers with small plots, the compact drill outsells the standard drill in dealer order books
Compact-drill orders peak in spring before sowing, unlike farmer orders that cluster after harvest
Stated price resistance rises sharply above the level repaid by two seasons of saved sowing labour
arguments.who_benefits: Small-plot growers gain sowing speed on land too small for a full drill; the firm gains margin on a low-new-tooling product using parts it already makes.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: They switch from hand sowing to a purchased implement only when the tool's price is repaid by saved sowing labour within one or two seasons on their plot.

justification.learned: allen-uspto-firm: for its first two decades the firm "limited itself to agricultural implements and machinery" - no consumer line evidenced. allen-uspto-components: seat, lever and trusses "also constituted the Planet Jr. line of cultivators" and workers "already had the skills and machinery" - capability and parts commonality, not demand. allen-uspto-seasonal: farmers "wait until they had sold a season's crop before ordering", leaving summer idle - a timing fact, not a consumer motive. So feasibility is supported; demand from individual buyers is unknown. Unread: allen-uspto-adreach, allen-uspto-rehire, allen-wp-slowseason.
justification.uncertain: Whether Allen already sells anything to individual gardeners versus only to farmers; what small-plot growers actually use instead of a full drill; willingness to pay at any price; whether any 1888 advertising reach to households exists. No financial data in the dossier. Repeated keyword searches on drills/small farms returned nothing new, so the evidence base is thin and any theory stays a hypothesis.
justification.why_next: The gate says theories 0 of at least 2, and the refusal itself says to add one with a different cause. The refused searches duplicated queries in already_tried, so searching again adds nothing. I add T1: a mechanism grounding why small-plot growers would buy a compact drill built from the parts described in allen-uspto-components, with the seasonal-ordering pattern in allen-uspto-seasonal as a proposed contrast in order timing. A second theory with a different cause (channel reach via dealers/catalogues, or summer capacity smoothing) must follow before evidence in allen-uspto-adreach and allen-wp-slowseason can be weighed against rival mechanisms.

examples.question: Should SIGVARIS GROUP develop a differentiated proposition for people who buy compression without a prescription, such as travellers or athletes, or keep its focus on medical compression? What evidence would justify either choice?

justification.learned: Read: sigvaris-about (own plants in Switzerland, France, Poland, US, Brazil; subsidiaries in 8 countries; distributors in 70+ countries — capability/route-to-market, not demand). sigvaris-medical-grade-worth (company argues prescribed medical-grade compression is not the same as "more affordable ones online", so cheaper non-prescription online substitutes exist and compete on price). sigvaris-review-travel (one wearer: "I have worn compression socks while traveling for years" but every sock was "scratchy and uncomfortable" — one customer's comfort complaint, not proof of purchase behaviour). No theories yet (0 of 2); nothing weighed, no test designed.
justification.uncertain: Whether non-prescription demand is real and how large: no source read so far shows anyone buying compression without a prescription, or the size/channels/costs of that segment. Also unknown whether SIGVARIS already sells direct to individual buyers. The four unread results (sigvaris-mordor-cep, sigvaris-mordor-channels, sigvaris-mordor-cost, sigvaris-travel-claim) may hold the independent market facts that would ground a theory.
justification.why_next: Two searches were refused for repeating the already-tried "compression socks fashion market" query, and the gate reports 0 of 2 theories. examples.question: It is 1989. Should Sam Farber develop a differentiated consumer proposition in kitchen tools for a specific use case, building on his housewares manufacturing experience? What evidence would justify that investment?

arguments.claim: People with weak, stiff or painful hands — arthritis sufferers and older cooks — physically cannot use ordinary kitchen tools comfortably, so a tool that grips and cuts without strength delivers real utility to them, and they will substitute it for a cheaper standard tool. A maker that designs to that constraint can charge a premium through ordinary housewares retail rather than a niche medical channel.
arguments.who_benefits: Older home cooks and people with arthritis or hand pain; secondarily anyone doing long repetitive peeling or chopping.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Their current peeler or knife slips, hurts or is abandoned mid-task, so they will pay more and switch brands to keep cooking independently.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Premium unit price over commodity utensils, repeat and gift purchases, and shelf space in mainstream housewares retail rather than a small medical-supply channel.
assumptions: Reduced grip strength is common enough among home cooks to be a viable segment
These buyers will pay a visible premium for comfort, not just take the cheapest tool
Mainstream retailers will stock a comfort-positioned tool without medical-style marketing
predictions: In a comparable in-store or mail-order offer, households with an older or arthritic cook buy the soft-grip peeler at a 20-30% premium over the standard one more often than households without
Sales concentrate in households with someone over 55 or reporting hand pain, not spread evenly across all cooks
Satisfaction and repeat purchase are highest among users who report hand pain before purchase

justification.learned: Read: oxo-ch15-research (Farber/Smart Design spoke with consumers, chefs and a New York arthritis group), oxo-modip-brief (brief was an affordable line usable by everyone, not solely arthritis; one shared handle across tools), oxo-smart-aha (company claim of a 1989 "aha" watching Betsey struggle with a peeler — assertion, not demand). No sales, price or market-size figures found; repeated "OXO sales 1989/1990" searches were refused as already tried and yielded nothing. Unread: oxo-census-65, oxo-ee-frame, oxo-ee-origin, oxo-modip-santoprene.
justification.uncertain: Whether any demand evidence exists at all: the arthritis-group consultation shows a design input, not purchasing behaviour, and no financial or market-size data is in the dossier. Also unresolved: whether the buyer segment is specifically people with reduced grip strength, or a universal "easier for everyone" appeal — the two design sources point in different directions (oxo-modip-brief vs oxo-ch15-research).
justification.why_next: The refusal states the stage is theories with 0 of 2 added. I will add T1, whose mechanism comes from the arthritis-group consultation in oxo-ch15-research and the handle decision in oxo-modip-brief, so those two sources can then be assessed and a rival cause built against them.

examples.question: It is autumn 2009. Should Probi develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its clinically documented probiotic strains, such as Lactobacillus plantarum 299v? What evidence would justify that investment?

justification.learned: Probi already reaches individual buyers indirectly: probi-fpj-1994 shows ProViva, with L. plantarum 299v, was launched in Sweden in 1994 by Skånemejerier (a dairy partner, not Probi itself); probi-bravo-strains (2009-09-02) shows Probi supplying HEAL9 and 8700:2 strains at ~1bn CFU/250ml to another firm's "world first" probiotic juice. So Probi's route to consumers is licensing/supplying, not own-brand retail. probi-r375-iron shows the EFSA opinion of April 2009 found no established cause-effect link for 299v and the 2010 refusal followed — a health-claim constraint on any differentiated use-case proposition.
justification.uncertain: No sources read yet on royalty economics, the value chain, or whether any strain has a unique, defensible consumer benefit (probi-nin-valuechain, probi-cis-royalties, probi-pr22-unique, probi-buoy-proviva are unread). Financial data is absent, so Probi's actual royalty rates, margins and consumer-facing volumes are unknown. Demand for a differentiated consumer proposition is entirely unmeasured in what I have.
justification.why_next: Stage is theories (0 of at least 2) and my repeated "Probi consumer brand retail 2009" searches were refused as duplicates; I need evidence on how value is captured before I can write a mechanism theory, so I next read probi-nin-valuechain, the only unread source describing the value chain.

examples.question: It is mid-1981. Should G.D. Searle develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its aspartame sweetener? What evidence would justify that investment?

justification.learned: Budgets: 2 searches (1 for challenge), €20,000/12-week test. Dossier: aspartame won July 1981 FDA approval as table-top sweetener and food additive, 'a minor victory' (searle-sfu-july1981); it 'lacked the bitter aftertaste of saccharin and eliminated 95.5 percent of the calories of sugar' (searle-sfu-aftertaste); Searle's base was prescription drugs (searle-sfu-dramamine). The 1984 CSM piece says 'the consumer never sees NutraSweet' (searle-csm-neversees), but post-dates the decision. Capability and regulation documented; demand, price sensitivity, retail route are not. Theories: none.
justification.uncertain: Whether Searle already reaches individual buyers beyond prescription medicines – the brief says find it, not assume. Whether any pre-mid-1981 public source shows consumer demand, repeat purchase or willingness to pay. The unread results (searle-csm-research, searle-nfu-patent) may bear on this, so I can't yet write a value-capture theory.
justification.why_next: Both refused calls repeated 'aspartame consumer survey 1981', already run twice, so no search repeats; two searches stay reserved for challenge_theory. The stage pointer wants a theory, but rule 2 says read before theorising, and searle-csm-research is unread and speaks to how Searle monetised the sweetener (value capture). Reading it unblocks two theories with different causes: consumer pull (people buy calorie reduction, so a branded table-top proposition earns a premium) versus supplier push (sweetener is an invisible ingredient, so value accrues via volume contracts with food and drink makers). My call reads searle-csm-research for exact wording before claiming either.

examples.question: It is early 2015. Should Osram Licht AG develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its LED and lighting technology? What evidence would justify that investment?

arguments.claim: Householders buy light as a commodity replenishment item: a lamp is bought when one burns out or a room is refitted, chosen on price, lumen/wattage match and immediate availability. A differentiated, higher-priced consumer proposition therefore does not change their choice, and value accrues to whoever owns shelf space and distribution scale rather than to the technology owner.
arguments.who_benefits: Mass retailers, wholesalers and distributors that control shelf space and can shop suppliers on unit cost; the manufacturer only insofar as it has listing scale and low unit cost.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: It does not: purchase is triggered by failure or refit, not aspiration; lumen and wattage are comparable at the shelf, switching cost is near zero, so buyers default to the cheapest adequate option.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Through volume, manufacturing cost per unit and retail listings — not through premium pricing or brand differentiation.
assumptions: Replacement lamps dominate Osram's consumer-facing volume in early 2015
Buyers can compare price and lumen output at point of sale
Osram's consumer reach is mainly lamps sold through third-party retail
predictions: In a 12-week retail/online test with parity placement, at least 85% of units in a lumen class go to the lowest-priced option
A differentiated consumer product priced at roughly 2x the standard lamp wins under 10% unit share
Asked to choose, a majority of replacement buyers pick standard over premium at comparable light output

justification.learned: Sources read show Osram already reaches individual buyers, but only through lamps: the LS segment "comprises luminaires for professional customers, products for consumers, as well as the service and solutions business" (osram-li14-consumer), and general lighting was ~40% of turnover, about €2bn in FY2015 (osram-ee-40). The April 2015 divestment announcement (osram-ldv-april) and the later sale postdate the decision date, so they are hindsight, not inputs knowable then. Nothing read yet shows consumer demand, price sensitivity or margins for a differentiated consumer product.
justification.uncertain: Whether households buying light treat it as a commodity replenishment or would pay a premium for a differentiated/connected proposition; Osram's consumer margin and channel position; what osram-tr-tesco and osram-wiki-sylvania contain (both unread). No independent study on consumer lighting purchase behaviour is in hand.
justification.why_next: Repeated identical searches ("Osram consumer LED work lights 2015") were refused as duplicates, and the stage now needs theories (0 of 2). Sources are enough to state a first mechanism, so I add T1 grounded in osram-li14-consumer: consumers replace lamps as a commodity, so value accrues to distribution scale, not to a differentiated proposition. A rival theory and the unread sources can then be weighed against it.

examples.question: It is late 1978. Should Texas Instruments develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its microprocessor and chip technology? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated TI microprocessor-based consumer product if it offers a clear, fun educational experience that demonstrates the technology's capabilities.

assumptions: Own-chip cost advantage translates into a visible retail price advantage.
Mass-market retailers will stock and price-promote a single standardised model.
Buyers do not need specialist advice or specialist stores to use it.
Narrow model range avoids the styling and variety problems that sank earlier consumer lines.
arguments.claim: Individuals buy a chip-based consumer product mainly on low price and single-purpose simplicity bought on impulse at mass-market retail, not on educational novelty; the firm that owns its chip supply and a mass retail shelf can win on cost and volume rather than on meaning or brand.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Vertical integration in semiconductors plus the existing mass-market retail channel (not specialist computer stores) and a deliberately narrow model range keep unit cost and distribution cost low, capturing value per unit sold at scale.
predictions: At comparable features, a lower-priced single-model offer sells more units than a higher-priced offer positioned as an educational experience.
Unit sales concentrate in mass-market retail and respond strongly to price cuts, whereas the education-led theory expects purchase intent to rise with educational framing at a similar price.
A wide multi-model range depresses sell-through per model even when average styling is better.
arguments.who_benefits: Price-sensitive households making low-risk impulse purchases and mass retailers wanting high-turnover items; the manufacturer earns thin per-unit margin but large volume from its own chip cost advantage and existing calculator shelf space.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: At a low enough price and with one obvious use, the purchase stops being a considered family investment and becomes an everyday buy, so volume rather than premium price carries the proposition.

justification.learned: Four sources read. ti-wiki-cal1967: TI invented the handheld calculator (1967) and the first single-chip microcontroller (1970), so it already sells to individual buyers, not only industry/government. ti-wiki-speak: a TI chip-based consumer product with speech was shown at the Summer CES in June 1978, so capability and a consumer route exist now. ti-994-channel: the route used was the calculator channel of mass-market retailers, \"not specialized computer stores\". ti-wiki-lcd: an earlier consumer attempt (LCD watches) failed on \"styling issues, excessive model variety, and price points\" — a channel/cost failure, not proof of no demand. T1 exists. Searches left 0, 1 held for challenge.
justification.uncertain: No source read shows unit sales, price, margin or retailer take-up, so demand and willingness to pay are unknown. Unread results ti-994-price, ti-994-loss, ti-pet-ces1977, ti-pet-frozen may bear on price and rival machines, but searches are exhausted. No independent study is in the dossier; every claim so far is a product fact or encyclopaedic account, so nothing yet shows why an individual buyer hands over money.
justification.why_next: The stage needs a second theory with a different cause; refusals were duplicate T1 and exhausted searches. I add T2, taking its distribution mechanism from ti-994-channel (mass-market retail, not specialist stores) and its failure mode from ti-wiki-lcd (model variety and price points beat styling). T2 must predict what T1 does not: T1 says educational framing lifts intent at similar price; T2 says volume follows price and shelf availability, so a cheaper single-model offer outsells a better-positioned educational one. Then I assess both against ti-wiki-speak and ti-994-channel, and spend the reserved challenge search on whichever looks stronger.

examples.question: It is late 1974. Should Statitrol Corporation develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its ionization smoke-detection technology? What evidence would justify that investment?

sources_read.statitrol-spr-commercial: 2016 (prize review; written after the decision date)

arguments.claim: Battery-powered ionization alarms turn smoke detection from a wired, contractor-installed building product into a self-installed household purchase in existing homes. The binding constraint is retrofit cost, so value shifts to whoever mass-produces cheap battery units and reaches retail shelves.
arguments.who_benefits: Owners of existing, unwired houses who would mount a unit themselves rather than hire an electrician to hard-wire one.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: With NFPA 74 (1974) and UL 217 (1974) legitimising battery models, a householder can buy and fit a unit without wiring or a contractor, turning a capital project into a shopping decision.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Low unit manufacturing cost plus access to mass-market retail shelf space; margin comes from volume at consumer price points, not from custom installation.
assumptions: Owner-occupied existing housing is the largest latent pool (proposed, not measured)
Units can be built and certified at consumer price points
Retail buyers will stock the category
Statitrol can reach shelf space itself or via a partner
predictions: Sales concentrate in owner-occupied existing housing rather than new construction
Retail-channel unit share exceeds builder or institutional share in early years
Units respond to retail price and shelf availability more than to code mandates

justification.learned: From statitrol-ieee-aec (AEC cleared residential use only in 1969), statitrol-ieee-nfpa74 (NFPA 74 revised 1974 for battery-operated models), statitrol-nist-ul217 (UL 217, first smoke-alarm standard, 1974), statitrol-spr-commercial (ionization detectors in hard-wired commercial use from the 1940s, impractical to retrofit into homes) and statitrol-ieee-sears1974 (a 1974 Sears distribution deal called decisive): by late 1974 a self-contained residential unit was technically and institutionally legitimate. No source read shows Statitrol's own route to individual buyers, nor any price, unit volume or demand figure.
justification.uncertain: Whether Statitrol sold to households at all in 1974; whether the Sears deal cited in statitrol-ieee-sears1974 belongs to Statitrol or to BRK/First Alert; statitrol-spr-origin is still unread; no financial, price or volume data anywhere in the dossier, so demand is unknown.
justification.why_next: Last call was refused as a repeat of the search "Statitrol ionization detector homeowner 1974", and the state records 0 of at least 2 theories, so the owed step is a causal mechanism, not another search. I add T1 grounded in statitrol-spr-commercial and statitrol-ieee-nfpa74, on the retrofit-cost mechanism; a rival with a different cause follows.

examples.question: It is late 2009. Should Martek Biosciences develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its algae-derived DHA omega-3 oil? What evidence would justify that investment?

arguments.claim: Shoppers cannot verify where DHA comes from, so a recognised algae-source ingredient logo substitutes for expert advice and lowers perceived risk of fishy taste or contamination. That trust shifts shelf choice toward logo-bearing packs, letting the ingredient owner earn a B2B premium and licence fee, so Martek captures consumer value through customers' brands rather than needing its own consumer product.
arguments.who_benefits: CPG brand owners (Minute Maid, Yoplait, Horizon) gain a defensible on-pack claim; Martek, which owns the life'sDHA mark, gains pricing power and pull; shoppers gain a shortcut for purity and vegetarian origin.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Health-conscious buyers at shelf face unverifiable source claims, so a familiar mark reduces search cost and perceived risk, changing which pack they pick and repeat-buy.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Through higher ingredient price and logo/licence terms charged to B2B customers, plus stronger negotiating position; not through retail margin on an own-brand product.
assumptions: Shoppers notice and trust the logo (awareness was 28% in 2008, per company release).
A meaningful share will pay a premium for algae versus fish-sourced DHA.
CPG partners accept an on-pack ingredient mark despite dilution of their own brand.
Martek can enforce logo use without controlling retail.
predictions: In matched packs with and without the logo, the logo variant wins a higher share of shoppers who see front-of-pack, with no difference when the logo is hidden (proposed test measure).
Buyers of premium juice/yogurt name DHA source as a purchase reason more often than price (proposed survey).
CPG customers accept a per-unit logo royalty, so Martek's consumer-facing revenue is B2B, not retail.

justification.learned: Martek's public record: formula supplements were 91% of sales in 2007 and 2009 (martek-mw-91pct); it already reaches shoppers indirectly via an ingredient brand, life'sDHA awareness 11%->28% among health-conscious consumers in two years (martek-fif-awareness), with its logo on Minute Maid, Horizon Organic and Yoplait packs (martek-fif-logo). All three are company assertions or aggregate observations; none shows a purchase driven by a Martek proposition. No financial data in dossier. Unread: martek-fpw-alliances, martek-ni09-infant, martek-ni10-99pct, martek-rfb-neuromins.
justification.uncertain: Whether logo awareness converts into purchase pull the ingredient maker can monetise, or whether CPG brand owners capture all of it. Whether Martek already has a consumer brand (e.g. Neuromins, see martek-rfb-neuromins) or only B2B alliances (martek-fpw-alliances). Underlying consumer demand is unknown from these sources: awareness is not buying.
justification.why_next: Last call refused because search_evidence repeated queries already in already_tried (DHA supplement consumer adoption 2009 and market-size variants); rerunning yields nothing. Stage says 0 of at least 2 theories, so the gap is causal, not further search. I add T1 from martek-fif-logo and martek-fif-awareness: shoppers delegate DHA-source trust to a familiar ingredient mark, so pull accrues to whoever owns the mark. A differently caused rival theory (benefit-led maternal segment, or commoditised supplement retail where marketers capture margin) follows next, then I read martek-rfb-neuromins and martek-fpw-alliances.

examples.question: Should Hilti develop a differentiated proposition for home users or hobbyists, beyond its existing professional offering, or leave that market alone? What evidence would justify either choice?

sources_read.hilti-consumer-market-size: unknown (written while the COVID-19 pandemic was ongoing)
sources_read.hilti-consumers-price-sensitive: unknown (written while the COVID-19 pandemic was ongoing)

assumptions: Occasional DIY use makes durability and service worthless to the buyer
Retail shelf presence costs less to serve than a direct salesforce
A stripped entry line can be sold without eroding the professional price umbrella
arguments.claim: Home users judge a power tool as a one-off cost against a single job, so their purchase is decided by shelf price rather than by brand, durability or service; a professional badge therefore commands no premium from them and only a genuinely cheaper tool wins their business.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Unit volume through retail at thin gross margin, with none of the service, fleet or consumable revenue that attaches to professional accounts.
predictions: Offered a cheaper Hilti-badged entry tool beside a premium Hilti tool, most home buyers pick the cheapest option, including a non-Hilti import
Stated willingness to pay a Hilti premium among home users is near zero in any survey
Widening retail distribution of premium-spec tools does not raise premium-unit sales to home users
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: They buy the cheapest tool that plausibly finishes the job; a Hilti badge alone does not shift them, only a lower sticker price near import levels does.
arguments.who_benefits: Price-sensitive homeowners doing occasional repairs, and any maker that strips cost out of the tool and sells it through mass retail rather than a direct salesforce.

justification.learned: Three sources read. hilti-b2b-reach: Hilti is "primarily a business-to-business supplier" that "hasn't done much to reach individual end users." hilti-consumer-market-size: consumers are "about half the size of the professional market." hilti-consumers-price-sensitive: "most consumers are very price sensitive... often opting for less costly imports over expensive professional-grade models." A large but price-driven consumer segment exists that Hilti does not reach; these excerpts do not show demand for a Hilti home proposition, which is unknown. Unread: hilti-craftsman-pro-label, hilti-direct-model, hilti-downscale-dilution, hilti-hd-exit, hilti-hd-rental. No theories filed yet (0 of 2).
justification.uncertain: Unknown: whether any home buyer would pay even a small premium for a professional badge, i.e. whether price is the only motive. Unknown whether Hilti could serve consumers profitably given its direct/service model, and what the Home Depot arrangement (hilti-hd-exit, hilti-hd-rental) shows about retailer willingness. hilti-consumers-price-sensitive is a general market statement, not Hilti-specific, and shows nothing about purchase behaviour of a Hilti-badged home product.
justification.why_next: The stage demands at least two theories with different causes. I add T1: home users buy tools as a one-off cost per job, so price decides and a professional badge yields no premium — mechanism drawn from hilti-consumers-price-sensitive, plus hilti-b2b-reach for why Hilti has no consumer franchise to leverage. A rival theory (pro-badge identity pull, or cost-to-serve economics of a service/fleet model) must follow, then assess_evidence against each using hilti-consumer-market-size and hilti-consumers-price-sensitive, and read hilti-direct-model and hilti-hd-exit to test the cost-to-serve and channel claims.

examples.question: It is early 2010. Should A123 Systems develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its lithium iron phosphate battery cells and packs? What evidence would justify that investment?

arguments.claim: A distinct group of technically engaged, environmentally motivated Toyota Prius owners wants plug-in capability from the car they already own rather than buying a new plug-in vehicle; they will therefore pay a large one-off premium for a factory-certified, warranty-safe conversion kit rather than a cheap uncertified one.
arguments.who_benefits: Existing Prius owners who value plug-in range, fuel savings and being an early adopter, and who prefer a certified kit to an uncertified garage conversion.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: A certified kit ($10,395, a123-nbf-price) buys plug-in function and regulatory/impact compliance (a123-osti-first) far cheaper than replacing the car, so owners act instead of deferring.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: A123 captures value as a branded aftermarket product with a premium price and a trained installer network, keeping pack and integration margin rather than selling cells to others.
assumptions: Buyers are a self-selected enthusiast niche reached through Prius forums, clubs and specialist installers, not mainstream retail.
Certification and warranty safety, not lowest price, are what unlock the purchase for this group.
Kit volumes stay small and high-margin; no mass-market scale is needed for value.
predictions: Kit purchase rate per 1,000 Prius owners reached is materially higher in enthusiast channels than in general retail advertising.
When shown a certified kit and an uncertified kit at half the price, most of this group still chooses the certified one.
Demand concentrates in CARB/emissions-sensitive states and among owners of 2004-2009 Prius models, not spread evenly across hybrid owners.

arguments.claim: Consumers will adopt MSA safety products for DIY and outdoor recreation if they perceive the products as reliable, brand trusted, and convenient to purchase through retail channels.
arguments.who_benefits: DIY homeowners and outdoor enthusiasts who need reliable safety gear and are willing to pay a premium for proven safety.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Growing DIY participation among younger generations and increased home improvement spending creates demand for safety products that are easy to find and trusted.

Price sensitivity will be low enough that a premium price is acceptable for safety gear.

Surveyed consumers will report higher purchase intent when the product is sold in a retail setting than when marketed directly to them.
Willingness to pay for a consumer-branded MSA product will be at least 10% above a comparable generic brand.

examples.question: It is late 2016. Should Microban International develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its antimicrobial and odour-control additive technologies? What evidence would justify that investment?

arguments.claim: Buyers cannot verify an antimicrobial or odour claim on a shirt, shoe lining or fridge interior, so they fall back on a familiar ingredient mark. A recognised additive brand lets a manufacturer turn an untestable credence attribute into a higher price; manufacturers therefore pay Microban for the mark as well as the additive, because the mark moves purchase toward their product.
arguments.who_benefits: Manufacturers in commoditised categories (textiles, footwear, housewares, appliances) that need differentiation, and Microban as owner of the mark.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Faced with identical, untestable claims from rivals, shoppers default to the marked product and accept a higher price, because the mark lowers perceived risk.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Additive volume plus ingredient-brand licensing or co-marketing fees from the 250+ partner manufacturers, funded by the retail premium on marked goods.
assumptions: Consumers recognise and trust the Microban name, which nothing I have read establishes.
The antimicrobial/odour benefit is unobservable in use, so trust cues drive choice.
Marked goods can carry a retail premium without making health claims that regulators would reject.
Manufacturers prefer paying for Microban's mark over promoting their own.
predictions: On matched product pairs, shoppers pick the Microban-marked item more often and at a higher price than an unmarked equivalent.
Partner manufacturers in credence-attribute categories (textiles, footwear) renew or pay for licensing more than those selling performance-verifiable goods.
Willingness to pay is higher when the mark is visible on pack than when the additive is undisclosed.

justification.learned: Sources read: microban-epa97-complaint (1997 EPA charged Microban with claiming treated consumer goods protect children from E. coli/Staph/Strep; approval covered only protecting the plastic); microban-thai-partners (250+ manufacturers incl. Tefal, GAP, Sharp, Dunlop differentiate via Microban); microban-thai-survey (Millward Brown: 80% believe antimicrobial products work, 66% would pay more). Microban reaches buyers only indirectly, via other brands; no direct route shown, no financials. Zero theories so far. Refusals came from repeating identical searches; microban-epa97-goods stays unread.
justification.uncertain: Whether the 66% stated willingness to pay is buying behaviour or politeness; whether consumers recognise or value the Microban name at all (no source read tests this); how far the 1997 EPA action constrains consumer-facing health messaging even in late 2016; what microban-epa97-goods adds about which goods were treated. Demand for any specific consumer proposition is unknown; I have seen no purchase data.
justification.why_next: The controller puts me at stage theories: 0 of at least 2, with add_theory, search_evidence and read_source open. Rather than re-running refused searches, I add the first causal mechanism, T1, built on microban-thai-partners and microban-thai-survey plus the verification problem implied by microban-epa97-complaint: buyers cannot test an antimicrobial claim, so a trusted ingredient mark carries the premium. A rival theory naming a different cause (regulator-imposed claims limits, or manufacturer-side pull) must follow before any assessment, and I will weigh it against microban-epa97-goods once that source is read.
