examples.question: It is late 1978. Should Texas Instruments develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its microprocessor and chip technology? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated TI microprocessor-based consumer product if it offers a clear, fun educational experience that demonstrates the technology's capabilities.

arguments.claim: In 1978 consumer electronics, individual buyers chose on price against adequate features and on availability in mass-market stores; differentiation by educational novelty did not command a premium, so a TI consumer product wins only by riding the chip cost curve down and holding shelf space.
arguments.who_benefits: Price-sensitive mass-market households buying their first electronic gadgets; TI benefits as the low-cost chip producer and mass-retail supplier, not as a premium brand owner.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Households switch only when a device crosses an affordability threshold; at parity of function they buy the cheaper unit on the shelf they already visit, so a price cut converts far more buyers than an added feature.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: TI captures value through volume and internal chip margin at falling unit cost, plus sell-through in existing mass-merchandiser accounts, rather than through premium pricing on novelty.
assumptions: Consumer electronics demand in 1978 was elastic to price at the low end.
Mass-merchandiser shelf space, not specialist retail, determined which products reached individual buyers.
TI could sustain lower unit cost than assembly-led competitors through chip integration.
predictions: At matched features, a lower-priced version outsells a feature-rich premium version by a wide margin in the same retail accounts.
A 10-20% price cut raises unit sell-through substantially more than adding an educational feature at constant price.
Products sold only through specialist or premium channels underperform those placed in mass-market accounts.

justification.learned: TI entered the decision date with real consumer capability and reach, not a blank slate: handheld calculator invented 1967 and first single-chip microcontroller 1970 (ti-wiki-cal1967); consumer sales through mass-market retailers rather than specialist computer stores (ti-994-channel); a microprocessor-speech product shown at the June 1978 Summer CES (ti-wiki-speak). T1 already encodes the educational-novelty mechanism. No source read so far contains sales, price, repeat-purchase or margin data, so consumer demand is unknown.
justification.uncertain: Whether 1978 individual buyers paid for differentiated features or for low price on adequate features. ti-wiki-lcd records that TI's watch line lost on styling, excessive model variety and price points, and ti-994-channel records mass-merchandiser distribution — both hint at price/channel as the dominant mechanism, but neither shows why buyers chose. No financial or unit-volume data exists in the dossier.
justification.why_next: The last two calls were refused because add_theory repeated T1's claim word for word, and the stage requires a second theory with a different cause (1 of at least 2). I add T2 built on ti-994-channel and ti-wiki-lcd: value in 1978 consumer electronics accrued to whoever cut price along the chip learning curve and held mass-retail shelf space, so buyers respond to price, not educational novelty. This is the opposite prediction to T1 and makes a discriminating test possible.

examples.question: It is 1983. Should Mag Instrument develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its machined anodized-aluminium flashlights? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Civilians will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition because they perceive the Maglite as a status symbol and a symbol of professional reliability, leading them to purchase multiple units for personal use.
theories.T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition because they need reliable, professional‑grade flashlights for outdoor recreation and home safety, and they will purchase multiple units to ensure availability.

arguments.reason: SYN-D (SIMULATED) reports a label printer reducing packing errors in a warehouse and explicitly states nothing about buyers was measured. T1 claims civilians will pay a premium because the Maglite signals professional reliability and status. An internal packing metric tests neither the motivation nor the purchase behaviour that T1 asserts, so it changes nothing; the theory stays open at 'likely' pending X1.

justification.learned: SYN-D is a SIMULATED warehouse test: a new label printer cut packing errors slightly, and the excerpt states "Nothing about wearers or buyers was measured." It bears on neither T1 (civilians pay a premium because the Maglite signals professional reliability and status) nor T2 (buyers pay for durable professional-grade lighting for outdoor and home use). Packing accuracy is logistics; it shows nothing about consumer motivation, purchasing behaviour or value capture. The real evidence is unchanged: mag-amw-standard, mag-fu-civilians, mag-fu-lawenforcement, mag-fu-stores, mag-nbc-mass, mag-npr-price. None shows civilian demand, so both theories stay open.
justification.uncertain: Whether any civilians in 1983 would buy a premium flashlight at all is unknown: mag-fu-civilians records design intent, not purchases, and mag-amw-standard records only institutional use. mag-npr-price shows the wholesale price was never raised, which constrains how far premium pricing (T1) or tool pricing (T2) fits the company's observed behaviour as of later accounts. Whether X1's stated willingness-to-pay would translate into deposits or repeat purchases is also untested; X1 has not been run.
justification.why_next: I act on SYN-D: it is irrelevant to T1 and T2, so revise_theory records T1 as kept, with no change to claim or to my 'likely' rating, because a simulated packing-error result cannot confirm or refute a claim about why civilians buy. With searches_left at 0, the only remaining discriminating step is X1 (Maglite Consumer Demand Test, the survey in the dossier), which pits T1's 20% status premium against T2's 15% tool-driven premium. Because X1 measures stated intent, not purchases, its result would bound - not settle - which mechanism operates.

examples.question: It is mid-1991. Should Diatek Corporation develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its infrared ear thermometer for hospitals? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Parents will adopt a consumer infrared ear thermometer if it is marketed as a quick, accurate, and safe alternative to mercury thermometers, because they currently struggle to read traditional thermometers.
theories.T2: Parents will adopt a consumer infrared ear thermometer if it is marketed as a convenient, non‑contact alternative to mercury thermometers, because they currently struggle to read traditional thermometers and prefer quick measurements.

sources_read.diatek-spinoff-device: 1991 (originally published; note on later acquisition added afterwards)

arguments.reason: SYN-D is a simulated warehouse exercise in which a label printer slightly reduced packing errors, and its own text states nothing about wearers or buyers was measured. It therefore says nothing about whether parents adopt an infrared ear thermometer because they cannot read mercury ones. T1's claim, assumptions and predictions are unchanged; no new market evidence arrived.

justification.learned: SYN-D is a simulated warehouse test: a label printer slightly reduced packing errors, and "Nothing about wearers or buyers was measured." Its mechanism (packing accuracy) and population (warehouse staff) do not overlap with T1's claim, that parents switch from mercury thermometers to an infrared ear thermometer because they struggle to read them. No belief moves. What supports T1 remains diatek-pm-zones (57.9% of parents owned a mercury glass thermometer, only 9.7% could read three thermometers) and, for feasibility only, diatek-jpl-market and diatek-spinoff-device (under-two-second measurement). None shows purchase behaviour; demand is unknown.
justification.uncertain: Whether the reading difficulty in diatek-pm-zones converts into willingness to pay a premium for an infrared ear thermometer; T1 and T2 make near-identical predictions (same 20-point threshold, differing only in cited reasons), so X1 distinguishes them weakly. No source read shows consumer price points, distribution or a mid-1991 consumer channel for Diatek; rival pressure from diatek-patent-rival (Thermoscan) is unassessed.
justification.why_next: Record T1 as kept against SYN-D: a simulated packing-error result cannot confirm or refute T1, so no change is the honest move rather than a spurious revision. Searches are exhausted (0 left) and SYN-D is the only new input, so the path stays with test X1, the cheapest way to observe parent choice behaviour. examples.question: Should Cotral Lab develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing hearing-protection offering? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Professional musicians will adopt custom-moulded hearing protection if it is marketed as a performanceenhancing tool that preserves sound quality while blocking noise, because they value accurate sound and are willing to pay a premium for a product that does not compromise their craft.
theories.T2: Sleep aid users will adopt custom-moulded hearing protection if it is marketed as a medical-grade solution that reduces sleep disruption caused by background noise, because they seek a product that addresses a specific health concern and are willing to pay for a solution that improves sleep quality.

arguments.reason: SYN-D is a simulated warehouse packing-error test and explicitly measured nothing about wearers or buyers; it cannot bear on whether musicians pay a premium for sound-preserving custom moulds. No real evidence in the dossier changes T1, which remains a hypothesis supported only by company assertions and partially undercut by bockstael-2015-looks.

justification.learned: SYN-D is a SIMULATED internal-logistics result: "a new label printer reduced packing errors slightly. Nothing about wearers or buyers was measured." It speaks to packing operations, not to why musicians or sleep-aid users would buy, so it bears on no theory and I keep T1 and T2 unchanged. What the real evidence shows is thinner than the position implies: T1 rests on company assertions (ctl-filter on in-house frequency filters, ctl-it1 on Bluetooth connectivity) plus bockstael-2015-looks, which reports that appreciation "mainly depended on comfort and looks, while differences in sound quality were less noticeable" — that cuts against T1's sound-quality mechanism.
justification.uncertain: Unknown and unresolved: whether musicians will pay a premium for custom-moulded protection, and whether sound quality (T1's mechanism) or comfort/looks (bockstael-2015-looks) drives their choice. T2 has no consumer evidence at all — ctl-filter and ctl-onsite only show capability. Cotral's reach to individual buyers is unverified; ctl-channel says sales go "primarily through direct channels to end-user companies", i.e. B2B. Real demand is unknown.
justification.why_next: SYN-D is irrelevant to T1 and T2 (packing errors are not purchase behaviour), so the next step is the discriminative test rather than more desk reading; searches are exhausted (0 left). Run X1: 300-respondent conjoint choice between a musician-framed and a sleep-aid-framed custom-moulded offer, comparing purchase intent and WTP. X1 separates T1 from T2 on consequential stated choice, and its outcome also tests bockstael-2015-looks' implication that sound quality matters less than comfort and looks. After X1, decide whether the €12,000, 6-week spend justifies a deposit-based pilot.
